title: Smart Self-Oxygenating Tissues for Organ Engineering
abstract: The engineering of organ sized tissues has the potential to address one of the greatest clinical challenges: the continuous and evergrowing donor organ shortage. However, large engineered tissues do not remain viable upon implantation as the limitation of oxygen diffusion causes massive anoxia-induced cell death. To overcome this, many researchers have attempted to expedite angiogenesis i.e., via implantation near vascular-rich tissues, co-implantation of endothelial cells, and release of vascular endothelial growth factors. These approaches still need improvement to prevent the imminent anoxia-induced cell death following implantation. Consequently, the local release or generation of oxygen has been considered by using oxygen-rich fluids such as perfluorocarbons. Although these approaches could indeed supply implants with oxygen for several hours, implant neovascularization typically requires several weeks. Consequently, despite numerous attempts, there currently still is no effective strategy to bridge the implanted tissues’ prevascular phase. This work addresses this crucial challenge by pioneering a unique solution that allows for the controlled generation of oxygen for an indefinite period, which will sustain the survival of large 3D tissues until the neovasculature is formed (Scheme 1). Our innovative solution is based on the transformation of the most abundant moleculewater) into the most needed substance (oxygen). To accomplish this, we hypothesize that a biodegradable and biocompatible solid-state electrochemical hydrolysis cell inside the tissue scaffold. The proposed technology will thus combine concepts of flexible electronics, catalysis, and 3D bioprinting to build the world’s first smart self-oxygenating tissues (SSOTs). The water will be converted to oxygen inside the BioGel via water-splitting using the 3D printed CP/GH/SNP electrode as the catalyst. This will be printed by an extrusion 3D printing technique to realize functional, implantable, and tether-free SSOTs. The ability to sustain life of the implantable SSOTs will be evaluated in vitro and in vivo to demonstrate the ability of our approach to sustain the survival of organ sized tissues. When successful, this technology will allow the unprecedented feat of producing oxygen for an indefinite time in a highly controlled manner within 3D tissues. We hypothesize that this technology can prevent the detrimental effects of anoxia or poor vascularization that hinder the in vivo use of organ-sized tissues. This yet unrealized feat represents a key stepping-stone towards the development of viable clinically sized engineered organs.

title: Development of Protist-Facilitated Transport for Sustainable Agriculture-Biotechnology
abstract: Protists are a diverse group of organisms that are defined as single-celled eukaryotes on the micrometer scale. Bacterivorous soil protists, such as the ones used in this study, are essential to their ecosystems by cycling nutrients for plants and increasing bacteria diversity through predation. These protists could potentially be used as transport vehicles for nano-encapsulated agrochemicals. In this study, three soil protists collected from the rhizosphere in eastern Connecticut are tested for their ability to move through a serpentine emulated soil device. The average biomass velocity of the protists as they move through the device is correlated with their nano-encapsulated agrochemical mass transport potential. Over 72 hours, although Colpoda steinii had the highest average velocity as it moved through the device, Colpoda lucida had the highest average biomass velocity due to its substantially larger size. Leptopharynx costatus had the lowest average velocity and average biomass velocity of the three. For future studies, Colpoda lucida is the most promising candidate.

title: Formulation of Magnetic Particle Imaging Tracers Using Flash Nanoprecipitation
abstract: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a novel and rapidly developing in vivo imaging method, which boasts significant advantages over traditional imaging methods (e.g. fluorescence or x-ray imaging). These advantages include the lack of ionizing radiation and tissue depth attenuation. MPI image quality depends on magnetic nanoparticle tracers, of which there is a large variety, including ferrocarbotran nanoparticles, magneto-liposomes, micelles, and individual PEG coated iron oxide nanoparticles (IONP). Here, we propose a new MPI tracer, which uses IONP clusters encapsulated by Flash Nanoprecipitation. Flash Nanoprecipitation is a size-tunable process which encapsulates hydrophobic agents within amphiphilic block copolymer membranes. This process is typically used in the realm of drug delivery to achieve controlled drug release rates, high drug loading (lower doses), and cell targeting (modifying block copolymer). By using FNP to encapsulate IONPs, however, we create magnetically controlled nanocarriers (MCNCs) comprised of IONP clusters with a block copolymer membrane. These MCNCs can range from 50 nm to150 nm in diameter. We show that clustering and encapsulating IONP into MCNCs has a negligible effect on MPI signal, and that MCNC tracers have comparable MPI resolution to unencapsulated IONP. By showing that FNP-encapsulated nanoparticles maintain their MPI properties, we pioneer the development of new MPI tracers that have greater capacity for tissue diffusion, efficient dosing, and cell targeting capability.

title: Characterization and Incorporation of Lipid Prodrugs into Liposomes
abstract: Targeted chemotherapeutic delivery is the process of delivering cancer drugs to diseased tissue in the body without harming healthy tissue. This project has three parts: drug synthesis, drug packaging, and drug delivery. This presentation will highlight the drug packaging portion of the project during which the synthesized prodrugs are packaged into liposomes and characterized to determine liposome size, drug incorporation, and stability. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) was used to determine the size of both the parent compound and the prodrug loaded liposomes. These sizes were monitored over the course of three weeks in order to determine the stability of both the parent compound and the pro drug loaded liposomes. The results from the DLS showed that the empty liposome sizes are between 100 nm and 120 nm whereas the prodrug-loaded liposomes were between 120 nm and 150 nm. These sizes stayed consistent over a three-week period. The drug incorporation was measured using UV-Visible Spectrophotometry (UV-VIS) and the results from the UV-VIS concluded that as concentration increased as the absorbance increased. The characteristic absorbance wavelengths were found at approximately 300 nm, 340 nm, and 410 nm. The outcome of these experiments confirms that the prodrugs have been incorporated into the liposomes and further research is required to determine the optimal concentration of prodrug to incorporate into the liposomes in order to maximize packing. The next step for this portion of the project is to characterize the rest of the prodrugs that have been synthesized.

title: Land of Hopportunity: Characterization of New Mexico-Grown Hops
abstract: Essential to the craft of brewing are hops: the flowers of Humulus lupulus which provide beer with bitterness, flavor and aroma. Containing a unique combination of bittering acids (α and β), essential oils, and polyphenols, each hop variety contributes to distinguishing brews. Recent research on hops has focused on the effects of growing location on the characteristics of the hops and the effects on the finished beers. Over the last two years, the NMSBrew team at New Mexico State University have been developing a technical assistance program to provide hop characterization analyses and best practices information to New Mexico hop farmers. This season, hop characterization focused on sensory evaluation, UV-Vis spectroscopy measurement of α and β acids, hop storage index based on moisture and temperature, and steam distillation of essential oils. Relatively new to the picture is Humulus lupulus neomexicanus, a variety of hops native to New Mexico with unique (but not always pleasant) aroma and flavor profiles, and relatively high levels of polyphenols. While some neomexicanus cultivars are available commercially, much more work is needed to understand the potential of this crop in the Southwest to support the local brewing industry.

title: In Vitro Model of Glioblastoma Using an Immortalized Cell Line
abstract: Glioblastoma brain cancer is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor that leaves its afflicted patients with a median survival rate of 1 year. This in vitro study seeds glioblastoma cells (U-87 MG line) into a microenvironment that mimics the brain’s. By placing glioblastoma cells into a soft hydrogel environment within a microfluidics chamber that receives electrical stimulation similar to that from neural activity, a phenotypic shift is expected to be triggered. This overall effort tests the hypothesis that such an in vitro model system can induce a phenotypic shift so that the immortalized U-87 cells more closely resembles primary tumor cells. 7 wt% Gelatin Methacrylate and 50,000 cells were seeded into a 10-mm diameter glass-bottom petri dish between carbon electrodes for electrical stimulation. Cells are expected to die in tumor treating-level fields, and after 19 h of stimulation, the treated cells displayed more cell death than the non-exposed control. It was seen that the experimental setup is functional as there was an obvious reduction in the number in living cells. By adjusting the field strength, it is expected that exposure to low frequency fields typical of brain activity, in addition to the soft substratum and microfluidic flow, will significantly alter expression of mechanoreceptors without inhibiting tumor cell proliferation.

title: Light Controllable Cell Patterning
abstract: Many different types of disease can cause damage to the heart’s veins and arteries. While some can be replaced with grafts of veins and arteries from other areas of the body, it is sometimes needed to find grafts from donors. Since finding tissue matches can be difficult and have complications, such as rejection, a method that grows these veins and arteries out of a patient’s stem cells would be optimal. One of the steps in growing veins out of stem cells is being able to pattern cells and achieve cell attachment in a specific location. A pattern was created on a bovine serum albumin coated slide using photobiotin, a photomask, and UV light. Cells were coated in sulfo-NHS-biotin, allowing them to attach to the patterned photobiotin. Biotinylated antibodies were also used to see if they decreased non-specific binding. Once the cells were incubated on the slides, a flow chamber was used to test the strength of their attachment. The use of antibodies was shown to help decrease unwanted attachment in addition to having stronger attachment than the sulfo-NHS-biotin coated cells. H9C2 and HUVEC cells were layered to recreate the functionality of real vein and artery tissue. This method was solely done with sulfo-NHS-biotin coated cells. The results of successfully patterning cells with strong attachment show promise for being able to one day grow a full vein or artery in a lab.

title: Electropermeabilization of Breast Cancer Cells to Calcium Ions Using Microsecond Electric Pulses
abstract: Microsecond pulsed electric field (μsPEF) exposure causes an influx of calcium (Ca 2+ ) that, in turn, sets off numerous signaling pathways. As a preliminary study, Ca 2+ uptake into breast cancer cells is measured in response to μsPEF exposure. By first finding the threshold number of pulses, duration, and voltage to increase permeability to Ca 2+ , it is predicted that these same conditions can be used to initiate downstream signaling cascades. Calcium ions play important roles within the cell acting as messengers that control crucial cellular responses that affect apoptosis, muscle contraction, gene transcription, metabolism, etc. Intracellular concentrations of Ca 2+ are very small compared to the extracellular matrix. This small concentration is essential for the signaling and communication processes to exist within the cell. When the cell is exposed to the μsPEF, pores form in the membranes of the cell causing a rise in concentration of Ca 2+ within the cell, interfering with calcium homeostasis. This rise activates calcium - ATPase which normally transfers Ca 2+ . It also activates an absorption of Ca 2+ into the mitochondria. Because of this gradient change, the mitochondria will collapse. With a lack of ATP being produced within the cell, cell death is triggered. By observing clear Ca 2+ uptake, it is shown that Ca 2+ dependent paths can be manipulated. In turn, Ca 2+ reliant cellular activities will be disrupted. Presently, we are exploring downstream responses to μsPEF with breast cancer cells .

title: Mimicking Molecular Interactions to Understand and Design Protein-RNA Regulation In Vivo
abstract: The Csr system is a model post-transcriptional regulatory network in E. coli. Two of its key components are the CsrA RNA binding protein and the CsrB small RNA (sRNA). CsrA is a global regulator protein that binds RNA. It affects the stability and translation of at least 30, but potentially hundreds of mRNAs 1 . On a phenotype-level, the CsrA protein impacts important cellular behaviors such as glucose storage and processing, synthesis of amino acids, biofilm formation, and motility 2 . The CsrB sRNA acts like a sponge and captures CsrA, which impedes CsrA’s ability to bind and regulate target mRNAs 3 . Pathogenic bacteria can flourish in host organisms and can cause diseases after entering the human body. In pathogenic species the Csr system has been shown to play a critical role in the virulence gene networks of Escherichia coli pathogens and is conserved in other organisms 4 . Escherichia coli is a food-borne pathogen that colonizes the large intestine. Escherichia coli can cause health issues such as hemolytic uremic syndrome and bloody diarrhea 5 . Understanding the interactions between CsrA-RNA binding sites in vivo is significant because studies like these could potentially reveal new drug targets and guide new approaches for the interruption of pathogenic phenotypes. title: Proteins Adsorbed to Fractal Aggregates for Enhanced Stability
abstract: Pharmaceutical companies manufacture medicines to remain stable and potent at their industry standard. The loss of potency during the storage and transport phases of these manufactured products negatively influences their efficiency and safety by compromising the structure of the proteins. In order for the medicines to retain their proper functionality during storage and transport, it is recommended that they are stored in conditions between 2°C and 8 °C (36°F and 46°F). Many companies use cold chains in order to keep these products within this specific temperature range during storage and transport. However those that cannot afford or do not have the technology to consistently store medicine within this temperature range lose the functionality of their medicines. A way to preserve functionality in these high heat and intense shaking conditions is to adsorb proteins onto silica fractals. Through the use of silica nanospheres, the proteins were able to be adsorbed onto the surface of the structures. Silica, which is a compound known for its heat resistance and fairly high melting point is an ideal candidate to assist in protecting the protein structure. The protein in use, Bovine serum albumin (BSA), is known to be highly adsorbent in nature. By adsorbing onto the silica fractals, the structure of the protein will become more stable while also increasing the protein’s temperature resistance.

title: The Study on the Hydro-Liquefaction Reaction of Lipid-Extraced Microalgae (LEM)
abstract: The Study on the Hydro-liquefaction Reaction of Lipid-extraced Microalgae (LEM) LEM are mainly composed of protein and polysaccharides. In order to make full use of the organic matter in microalgae, and improve the application channel and comprehensive value of microalgae, the hydro-liquefaction reaction behavior of LEM was studied. The influences of solvent types and reaction conditions including reaction temperature, reaction time, solid-liquid ratio and initial hydrogen pressure on the yield of liquid-phase products were investigated, and found that the conversion of LEM hydro-liquefaction reaction increases with the increase of solvent polarity, and ethanol is the most suitable solvent. The yield of the liquid-phase products can be increased by increasing reaction temperature, reaction time and ethanol dosage. The optimum conditions for LEM hydro-liquefaction reaction were reaction temperature 290 °C, reaction time 30 min, initial pressure of hydrogen 3 MPa, and solid/liquid ratio 1:10 (w/v). Under the optimum condition, the yield of the liquid-phase products was 65.72%. The effects of the type and amount of ionic liquids (ILs) on the yield of the liquid-phase products from LEM hydro-liquefaction reaction were studied. It was found that when the amount of [Bminm] Cl was 1.0wt%, the highest liquid-phase products yield was obtained. By comparing the characterization of liquid products prepared in different catalytic systems, it was found that ILs/nickel-based catalysts could improve the liquefaction reaction degree and calorific value of LEM. However, the liquefied products of LEM hydro-liquefaction reaction are not suitable for preparing high calorific value biofuel oil because of the low H/C ratio, high N/C ratio and low calorific value.

title: Development of an Inexpensive Fine Particle Stabilized Aqueous Nitrogen Foam System for Enhanced Oil Recovery
abstract: Development of water flooding is the pivotal method in the process of utilization of global oil and gas resources, which is studied by more and more engineers and scientists all over the world. However, with the development of water flooding, it is inevitable that oilfields will enter the extra high water cut stage. Currently, the oil recovery rate by water flooding is generally less than 40% on a global scale. Therefore, how to continue improving oil recovery in the extra high water cut stage is an urgent problem to be solved. Especially with the fluctuation of oil prices in recent years, exploring inexpensive and high-efficient oil displacement system is a key measure to overcome this problem. It is worth noting that foam, as an efficient oil displacement system, has been gradually accepted on a global scale. However, this technology is limited by the cost of the foam stabilizer and its foam stabilizing ability, which is difficult to be promoted on a large scale. In this work, the composite clay and fine particles which are from coal combustion are compounded and used as an inexpensive foam enhanced system. The experimental results show that fine particles can significantly improve the stability of foam, and can make the bubbles stabilized in the porous medium for a long time, which overcomes the Oswald effect between the bubbles to some extent and weakens the separation of gas and liquid. Besides the addition of particles also reduces the volume of the bubbles, which makes the bubbles more rigid, thereby increasing the apparent viscosity of the foam and improving the sealing ability of the foam in the formation. Therefore, fluid mobility capacity can be effectively controlled by special foam in the extra high water cut stage. Moreover, the sweep efficiency of the oil-displacing agent around the foam is remarkably enhanced, meanwhile the addition of the particles also enhances the washing efficiency of the foam as the oil-displacing agent.

title: Development of Falling Thin Film Liquid Phase Electrolyzer for CO 2 Reduction
abstract: Anthropogenic CO 2 emissions are on the rise despite rapid advances in renewable energy. This discrepancy can be attributed to the difficulty in replacing established technologies, which are heavily reliant on fossil fuels. Electrochemical CO 2 reduction offers a promising solution to reduce industrial CO 2 emissions by enabling the production of carbon-negative and profitable industrial chemicals. For electrochemical reduction to be feasible, the electrolyzer needs to achieve several figures of merit: low cost, high current density, high energy efficiency and stability. Liquid phase electrolyzers (LPEs) confer an advantage over gas phase electrolyzers (GPEs) by operating at higher current densities, which may lower capital costs. Additionally, LPEs can produce a wide variety of value-added carbon products such as plastic monomers provided that a selective and active catalyst can be discovered; GPE products are restricted to C 1-3 products with a low boiling point which typically also have low market value. The primary barrier to industrially scaling up LPEs is the occurrence of liquid flooding of gas channels that impairs the mass transport of CO 2 to the catalyst. However, the chlor-alkali industry has developed falling film electrolyzers to circumvent the pressure differential at the root of the flooding problem. This technology is considered the state-of-the-art in large scale electrolyzers. In a falling film configuration, the electrolyte runs from the top of the cell down by action of gravity, the small liquid volume reduces the hydrostatic pressure, eliminating differences in pressure over the height of the electrode. Drawing from this established configuration, we created an electrolyzer prototype using 3D printing that does not suffer from flooding. Using 3D printing, we also created a proprietary percolator design which increases electrolyte mixing while optimizing the ionic conductivity. The design ensures continuous wetting of the entire electrode surface with minimal blocking of catalyst surface area. The architecture of the cell prevented fluid flooding of the catalyst, reduced cell resistances resulting in enhanced current densities; thereby indicating that this design is advantageous for scaling to industrial dimensions for CO 2 electrolysis.

title: Design of Pumped Hydro Energy Storage System for Smart Grid Application
abstract: While countries are pushing their goals of producing only renewable (green) energy, engineers need to solve the challenge that arises by relying on such resources - irregularity. Renewable energy sources need plenty of storage to ensure that the grid can function in their absence. This is where the idea of a pumped hydro energy storage (PHS) system saves the night! A pumped hydro system works like an energy reserve; when the demand for electricity is not met by the traditional generators or renewables, the PHS system powers up and generates electricity whereas when the demand is low and the production is high, for example during the day or during windy periods, the turbine utilizes the excess energy to pump water up an elevation and store it as potential energy. The objective of this project was to design a PHS system through the development of a model and optimization of parameters to maximize net present value. Traditional grids do not have the capability of getting feedback from the consumers. In such cases, Smart grids bring the feedback element into the equation. This is utilized to predict the fluctuations in the prices of electricity and channel the excess energy that is otherwise lost in the grid. Additionally, a demand response study provides day-ahead prices of electricity for an interval of time. The characteristics of the smart grid in conjunction with the day-ahead electricity prices are used by the PHS model to generate an operation schedule for the plant that will maximize profit. The model repurposes abandoned quarries as reservoirs. Using the concepts of linear programming and receding horizon (model predictive control), an estimate for reservoir capacity and profit from revenue was obtained. An economic analysis was performed on this model to approximate an initial capital investment in this project. Losses were calculated to simulate the plant operation which was utilized in the code. Overall, the investigation suggests the feasibility of a PHS in a quarry system.

title: Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Micro-Algae to Produce Liquid Biofuels
abstract: Algae biofuel is a carbon neutral alternative to fossil fuels, which are the main source of carbon dioxide emissions. Biocrude oil can be extracted from algae through hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), but the produced product contains heteroatoms such as oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen. However, the biocrude oil can be upgraded into higher quality oil using heterogenous catalysts. The green algae, Micractinium Immerum , was hydrothermally liquefied at 300 ℃. The crude oil was then separated from other fractions using dichloromethane as the solvent. After HTL, the biocrude from Micractinium was upgraded with catalysts MO 2 C, HZSM-5, and Pt/C at 350 and 400℃ using hydrogen at 1000 psi. The upgraded oil’s elemental composition was measured using an elemental analyser. The products were analyzed for high heating value using a bomb calorimeter. Although all the three catalysts decreased the heteroatoms in the crude oil at these process conditions, the HZSM-5 catalyst performed the most effectively, while the Pt/C catalyst yielded the highest heating value. By improving the energy density, algal-derived fuel may become a competitive alternative to fossil fuels and ultimately reduce additional carbon emissions.

title: Effective Modeling of the Coal Combustion in Fluidized Bed Reactor Using the Aspen Plus.
abstract: Despite numerous attempts to replace fossil fuels with biomass for the energy production to reduce the environmental pollution, coal remains one of the main sources of energy contributing to the 25% of the world’s energy generation. The need to study the coal combustion process remains crucial to develop its usage to an efficient level. For this purpose, several models of the coal combustion process were studied and developed both experimentally and computationally using different types of coal and different types of reactors like the fixed and fluidized bed. However, these works are insufficient to design a general model of the coal combustion process due to their specificity in process and design. Therefore, it is important to design the process simulations for the coal combustion that reproduce the real behavior of the process. This became possible with the recent introduction of new tools by Aspen Plus software that proposes a new built-in operation model for the design of the fluidized bed processes. Herein, we design and study the coal combustion process applying the novel tool at different operational conditions, i.e. temperatures and coal/air flow rates. The simulation explores the hydrodynamics and kinetics of the combustion process. To validate the performance of the simulations, the fuel combustion process was performed on a pilot-scale fluidized bed combustor using the Ekibastuz coal, a type of low-grade Kazakhstan coal. Obtained experimental results were used for the validation and fine-tune the Aspen Plus model. Eventually, it was noticed that both models are in a close agreement representing accurate results for the gas compositions, including SO x and NO x measurements, and the hydrodynamics of the reactor. Moreover, to examine the temperature and feed flow rate effect on the process efficiency and flue-gas compositions several sensitivity analyses were performed. Taken together, work assist in the development of an efficient and accurate model for the coal and biomass co-combustion processes designed using the fluidized bed reactor.

title: Fabrication and Evaluation of Lightweight Proton-Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells
abstract: The objective of this study was to create lightweight proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) by replacing traditional bi-polar plates with combinations of polycarbonate (PC) flow channels and metallic mesh current collectors. The concept was based on previous work in literature, which demonstrated the effectiveness of using fuel flow channels fabricated from thermally imprinted PC film. While the cited literature uses a heated hydrostatic pressing technique, this study demonstrates that a similar thermal imprinting method using a hydraulic press, heating blocks, and a two-piece die assembly can also produce effective flow channels. This study involved the testing of four PEMFCs: one commercially available cell used to collect control data and the remaining three made by replacing components of the control cell with lab-fabricated ones. After cell testing, qualitative conclusions were made based on the performance of each cell. Fuel cell performance is explained with the aid of measured polarization curves. It was concluded that a serpentine flow channel design operates more effectively than other unchanneled designs, and because a silver mesh current collector far outperforming current collectors made with stainless steel, it was affirmed that current collector electrical conductivity plays a major role in PEMFC power output capacity. Also noted in the study was a progressive decrease in performance across tests of the control cell, speculated to be a result of membrane-electrolyte assembly (MEA) degradation due to extensive use. This observation along with the those which led to the previously stated conclusions open the door for further testing and research into cell performance as it relates to cell design.

title: Identifying Optimal Conditions for Aluminum Catalyzed Conversion of Glucose to HMF in NMP
abstract: HMF is a desirable chemical that can be produced from renewable and lignocellulosic materials and which has several useful applications, including biofuels and polymer synthesis. Aluminum catalyst L Ph AlMe 2 ( 2e ) was explored as a method of glucose isomerization to fructose and subsequent fructose dehydration to HMF in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP). Reaction temperature and the addition of co-catalysts were studied to identify reaction conditions that maximize glucose conversion to HMF. Glucose and catalyst 2e were reacted in NMP and analyzed via HPLC to study glucose to fructose isomerization. A reaction temperature of 120 °C provided the highest yield of glucose to fructose in NMP (yielding an 80% fructose selectivity), however fructose was found to degrade in the presence of catalyst 2e in NMP at all temperatures. Co-catalysts P 2 O 5 and Nickel (II) Chloride were added to the reactions to induce HMF production in NMP. P 2 O 5 is a strong dehydrating agent and has been previously shown to improve fructose to HMF conversion. Starting with glucose in NMP, P 2 O 5 led to glucose conversion to unwanted by-products and no fructose or HMF was formed. Nickel (II) Chloride was considered as a co-catalyst because the halide anions created when in NMP allow fructose to be easily converted to HMF. Nickel (II) Chloride was found to give a glucose conversion of 55% along with an HMF selectivity of 24%. This reaction should be further optimized to effectively utilize Nickel (II) Chloride in NMP to improve the conversion of glucose to HMF. Further improvements in this reaction increasing selectivity of HMF, combined with harvesting glucose from cellulose, would allow industrial scale production of HMF from lignocellulose.

title: The Effect of Non-Alkanes on the Gelation and Thermodynamic Properties of Petroleum-like Solutions
abstract: Wax deposition in deep sea oil pipelines is an important and costly issue in the petroleum industry. The wax that forms in these pipelines is composed primarily of n -alkanes. However, there are many other components within the wax that can alter its crystallization and agglomeration properties. This work focused on the role of aromatics on the crystallization properties of the model waxy crudes. These waxes were composed of one or two n -alkanes, either C 28 , C 32 , or C 36 , mixed with either a single ringed aromatic durene or the polycyclic aromatic compound phenanthrene in a dodecane (C 12 ) solvent. Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) showed that the cloud points of these model waxes were not affected by the addition of aromatic molecules at low concentrations, but at high concentrations phenanthrene caused an increase in cloud point because the phenanthrene molecules would crystallize out of solution first.

title: Electrochemical and Thermal Analysis of an Ionic Liquid Based Solid Polymer Electrolyte
abstract: Lithium Ion Batteries (LIBs) have emerged as the leading technology in energy storage, with potential applications ranging from consumer electronics to hybrid vehicles and storage of energy produced by photovoltaics. State-of-the-art LIBs utilize a liquid electrolyte that poses issues such as flammability, potential leakage from battery casings, and dendrite growth when used with lithium metal. Solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) show promise in replacing liquid electrolytes, as they offer decreased flammability and the potential for dendrite prevention, enabling the use of lithium metal. However, SPEs are often hindered by low ionic conductivities and poor contact with electrodes. In this work, a SPE is proposed that consists of a high molecular weight polyethylene oxide (PEO) matrix with an ionic liquid and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) as plasticizers. A range of different compositions of SPE were fabricated and their electrochemical and thermal properties were characterized using cyclic voltammetry, electrical impedance spectroscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry. Our experiments demonstrated a high lithium conductivity and wide electrochemical and thermal stability windows for the electrolyte. Cycling cells, constructed using lithium metal and a composite Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) electrode, demonstrated high coulombic efficiency and minimal capacity fade through cycling at both elevated temperature and room temperature. As a whole, the SPE compositions with a higher ratio of ionic liquid to polymer showed higher conductivity and improved cycling performance. These electrolytes with high ionic liquid content show promise as safe, stable, and conductive alternatives to liquid electrolytes for lithium ion batteries and are also commercially relevant due to their ability to cycle at a wide range of temperatures with commercially available electrodes.

title: Novel Electrochemical Technique to Track Rapid Decay of Redox Active Species
abstract: The availability, abundance, and energy density of fossil resources have driven progress over the last century leading to dramatic improvements in quality of life worldwide. However, to avert catastrophic climate change, there is an increasingly urgent need to reduce carbon emissions without stifling economic growth. Deep decarbonization necessitates mass deployment of renewable technologies, such as wind and solar photovoltaic, to displace existing fossil generation. Though increasingly inexpensive, the inherent difficulties in converting the intermittent output of renewable installations into reliable, dispatchable power sources represents an important constraint and motivates research into storage technologies to buffer the intermittency without significantly increasing the cost of electricity. Redox flow batteries (RFBs) hold promise for long duration electrochemical energy storage by employing permanganate, a low cost redox active species. However, this species auto discharges to manganite and oxygen, introducing a potential flammability concern. Due to the rapid decay kinetics, typical ultramicroelectrode (UME) cyclic voltammetry cannot be employed and so a novel electrochemical technique is developed and validated to track rapidly decaying electrochemical species. In this work, a reducing potential is held in a permanganate electrolyte and the limiting current is tracked continuously. From current, a concentration can be determined and fit numerically to a general rate equation. The decay order was found to be close to second order with the rate constant near 40 M -1 s -1 , in close agreement with experimental observations. These findings are corroborated with UV-vis spectrometry.

title: High Energy Density Flexible Aluminum-Air Fuel Battery Performance
abstract: This article mainly talks as a new type of energy storage system, metal-air battery has great development potential. At present, there are two main problems in the development of aluminum -air battery: one is the corrosion of aluminum anode to produce hydrogen, and the other is the low ORR activity of air cathode. The most important factor determining the activity of air electrode is the ORR activity of cathode catalyst. The starting point of this paper is to improve the activity of cathode catalysts. Compared with traditional noble metal platinum-based catalysts, perovskite catalysts have low cost and high catalytic activity, thus becoming a research hotspot. The innovation of this paper is to replace La element at a position of LaMnO 3 perovskite oxide with appropriate Sr element, so as to improve its catalytic activity. In the experiment, in order to improve the conductivity of perovskite catalyst, a certain proportion of conductive carbon black was added. Finally, using hydrophilic conductive carbon cloth as catalyst substrate, flexible electrode was prepared, and flexible aluminum air battery was assembled by combining aluminum anode and flexible solid electrolyte membrane. title: Computational Fluid Dynamics Analysis of Polymer Elasticity and Pore Morphology on Residual Oil Saturation
abstract: Abstract Polymer flooding is a widely used Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) method that uses polymer solutions to increase sweep efficiency by decreasing the water/oil mobility ratio. Viscoelastic polymers have shown potential in reducing residual oil recovery, primarily due to the additional forces exerted such as normal stress forces, which help overcome capillary forces. In this work Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were used to analyze the flow of viscoelastic polymers both within a single pore throat and a network of pores. Simulations were carried out in two pore geometries, namely a pore centered geometry and a constriction geometry similar to that used by Afsharpoor et al.[1], for viscoelastic fluids with viscosities of up to 50 cP and relaxation times of up to 0.2 s. The relative effect of the various forces, specifically the normal forces, on the fluid’s ability to mobilize the residual oil within the pore is investigated. Moreover, CFD was used to analyze the performance of the viscoelastic fluids in 5 different porous media geometries with different pore heterogeneities, pore connectivity, pore shape and tortuosity, and the performance of the viscoelastic polymer properties on the enhanced oil recovery, breakthrough time and fluid trapping within the 5 different porous media geometries was investigated. title: Natural Gas Sweetening By Membrane Cascade Using a Standardized Model
abstract: Natural gas prices are at a low due to high availability which has driven several companies to consider using C1 chemistry to generate petroleum products and petrochemicals, particularly from stranded gas reserves that are typically flared. [1] Processes which aim to take advantage of these resources must be modular, but have similar requirements to centralized processing plants in terms of required feedstock and product purities. Membrane cascades, which use a series of interconnected, permi-selective membrane modules to separate fluid mixtures, have been proven for removing contaminants from natural gas, mainly CO 2 . [2] However, most commercial process simulators lack the models needed to simulate gas separation membranes. As part of the RAPID Center for Process Modeling’s effort to provide models and recommendations to the engineering community, a “membrane separation toolkit” has been developed to standardize simple membrane modeling. A test case involving the purification of 25 MMSCFD of CH 4 laden with CO 2 as the primary impurity using a standard cellulose acetate membrane was developed to demonstrate the use of the toolkit. The cascade was optimized with respect to the stage operating pressures, temperatures, and cuts to produce pipeline quality natural gas containing ≤ 3 % CO 2 by minimizing OPEX and maximizing the produced volume of salable gas. title: Cold Flow Properties of Biodiesel Blended with Model Diesel Solutions
abstract: Biodiesel is widely becoming a viable alternative to petrodiesel due to its carbon neutrality and the sustainable future it offers. However, the use of biodiesel is inhibited by its inferior cold flow properties, specifically, its higher cloud point. This issue is problematic in colder climates, because the biodiesel will solidify at temperatures of around 0 to -10°C, approximately 20-40°C higher than petrodiesel. While the cloud point of biodiesel can be depressed by varying the fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) composition, it is important to consider other viable strategies for cloud point depression. One such method is to mix biodiesel with petrodiesel, creating blends with favorable cold flow properties. This work considered blends of biodiesel and petrodiesel to understand the effect blending has on cold flow properties. Model diesel solutions were created using decane, dodecane, hexadecane and mesitylene to investigate the influence of different diesel components on important cold flow properties. These model diesel solutions were mixed with biodiesel to create B0, B25, B50, and B100 fuels, the phase transitions of which were studied using differential scanning calorimetry. The experimental cloud points of blends were used to consider the effect of the biodiesel fraction as well as the components in the model diesel solution. Additionally, the heats of crystallization were measured to determine the heats of mixing corresponding to each blend. Furthermore, this work used ideal solution theory to predict the cloud point, and consequently study how the blends deviate from ideal solution behavior. The difference from ideality was considered based on the biodiesel fraction and the model diesel solution components.

title: Subsurface Modelling of Deep Direct-Use (DDU) Geothermal on the West Virginia University Campus - Morgantown, WV
abstract: Subsurface modelling of Deep Direct-Use (DDU) geothermal on the West Virginia University Campus - Morgantown, WV Kevin B. Donnelly 1 , Nagasree Garapati 1 , Yingqi Zhang 2 , Pierre Jeanne 2 1 Department of Chemical and Biomedical Engineering, Benjamin M. Statler College of Engineering and Mineral Resources, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV 26506. 2 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, 1 Cyclotron Rd, Berkeley, CA 94720 The north-central region of West Virginia hosts a unique geological opportunity for the development of deep direct-use (DDU) geothermal energy. Being in the midst of this region, West Virginia University’s (WVU) Morgantown campus could potentially supply its heat from DDU geothermal in an effort to increase renewable energy on campus. This work features the results of simulations done for a subsurface reservoir using TOUGH2/EOS1, a program specifically developed to simulate coupled transport of water and heat in geothermal reservoirs. Reservoir behavior (pressure, temperature) over 60 years of production time is analyzed. In order to achieve a more accurate pressure profile at well bores, a radial mesh is used around injection and production well bores in the simulations. Reinjection temperatures and flow rates were varied for different well configurations to analyze their effects on the reservoir productivity. The reservoir behavior is analyzed through temperature and pressure contour maps created at various time periods within the 60-year timeframe. Longevity of the reservoir decreased with increased mass flowrate and lower reinjection temperatures. Comparing single production wells to multiple production wells showed that at the same total production flow rate, single production wells experienced faster thermal breakthroughs and higher-pressure drop than the multiple production wells. These results from numerical simulation help in designing the optimum well configuration. title: Renewable Power Generation through Reverse Electrodialysis
abstract: Renewable Power Generation through Reverse Electrodialysis Abstract: The rapidly growing energy demand along with the extensive use of the limited fossil fuels and the consequent climate change issues drives the search for alternative energy sources. Recent estimates suggest that approximately 40% of global electricity demands can be met by capturing the potential energy contained in the mixing of seawater and freshwater at coasts, by utilizing the salinity gradient, separated by a semi-permeable membrane to derive a potential difference. The chemical potential difference between salt and freshwater generates power which is around 2.3 MJ/1 m 3 of river water. The gross power potential of this unconventional and unrevealed energy source is estimated to be 2.4-2.6 TW when the average discharges of all rivers were taken into account. Salinity Gradient Power (SGP) is environmentally sound as well as a sustainable method of power generation from the reversible mixing of two kinds of water with different salt concentrations. The Gibbs free energy that is released when salt water and freshwater partially mix, can be captured in a process called Reverse Electrodialysis (RED). In RED, a series of anion exchange membranes (AEM) and cation exchange membranes (CEM) are alternately stacked between two electrodes, thereby creating adjacent low concentration compartments (LCCs) and high concentration compartments (HCC), which are fed by two aqueous salt solutions of different salinity. The salinity difference on either side of the membranes initiates selective transport of ions across ion-exchange membranes towards the electrodes. The ionic current in the cells is converted into electricity by redox reactions at the electrodes. Literature data show that the obtained power density increases progressively with higher salinity gradients, despite lower membrane permselectivity, as a result of reduced electrical resistance at higher concentrations. Significant improvements in power and current generation were obtained by using brush current collectors. The large surface area of these brushes reduced electrode resistances by increasing charge transfer to/from the carbon particles. In the present work, the effect of the spacer (which determines the distance between the stack membranes) thickness on power density was evaluated. Results revealed that lowering the spacer thickness from 500µm to 200µm improved the power density up to 32%. Moreover, the effect of flow velocity was also evaluated and critical velocity was found to be ~2.5 cm/sec.

title: Evaluating the Impacts of Extended Coordination to the Uranyl Cation Using a Tetracarboxylic Acid Ligand
abstract: Two novel crystal structures containing tetrahydrofuran-2,3,4,5-tetracarboxylic acid (THFTCA) and the uranyl (VI) cation were synthesized and characterized with single crystal X-ray diffraction and Raman spectroscopy. THFTCA is important in separating uranium from other actinides and is used in the disposal process of radioactive waste. This study analyzed how the coordination environment of the uranyl cation impacted its interactions with THFTCA. Two uranyl structures were isolated. The first, a simple monomer with piperazine acting as a charge balancing counter-cation. The second a framework with two unique uranyl environments and a sodium dimer. Within the uranyl structures, an increase in complexity was observed when a non-organic counter-cation was introduced, which contributed to the formation of a 3D framework. Shifts in the Raman spectra were analyzed to determine vibrational differences that resulted from the coordination of THFTCA to the uranyl cation.

title: Improved Surface Passivation of Halide Perovskite Quantum Dots Using 5-AVA
abstract: Shifting the world from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources is becoming increasingly vital, and requires efficient and low cost renewable electricity generation. One emerging class of solar cell which could drive this change is halide perovskite solar cells, a solution-processable semiconductor material. State-of-the-art perovskite solar cells have surpassed 25% efficiency, but further efficiency, and perhaps more importantly stability, gains appear to be tied to defects at the material’s surface. Halide perovskite quantum dots (QDs) are an elegant vehicle for studying surface properties due to their high surface to volume ratio. In this study, three different halide perovskite quantum dots (~7 - 9 nm in diameter) were synthesized: CsPbI 3 , CsPbBr 3 , and FAPbI 3 along with alloys of the form Cs 1-x FA x PbI 3 and CsPbI 3(1-x) Br 3x . In a typical synthesis, the QDs are capped by amine and carboxylate ligands which are quite labile and form a dynamic QD surface. These as-synthesized quantum dots were treated with the iodide salt of the bifunctional ligand molecule 5-aminovaleric acid (5-AVA) to better passivate the QD surface. CsPbI 3(1-x) Br 3x resulted in a quantum yield increase by 300% following 5-AVA treatment while other QD alloys had little to no change. These experiments provide insight into the complex surface chemistry of varying halide perovskite materials. Ultimately, improved surface passivation of QDs could lead to a better understanding of the surface properties of halide perovskites in general and thus improve optoelectronic devices.

title: Microemulsions in Acidic and Alkaline Environments As Electrolytes for Energy Storage
abstract: Redox Flow Battery (RFB) technology can store a large amount of energy as chemical energy that can later be discharged on demand. Intermittent renewable energy sources, such as solar or wind power, are becoming more common, thus the need for state-of-the-art batteries is increasing. A main component of RFBs is the electrolyte solution that is used to store energy. The most common type of RFB is the vanadium RFB (VRFB), in which vanadium serves as the charge carrier. Disadvantages of VRFBs are the high cost of vanadium, crossover of vanadium, and corrosion from sulfuric acid. In this work, microemulsions are explored as the electrolyte solution in RFBs. Microemulsions use surfactants to stabilize two immiscible liquids, thus increasing the number of redox pairs that can be incorporated into the electrolyte solution by solubilizing hydrophobic charge carriers. In this work, the microemulsion system used consists of water, Tween-20 (surfactant), 1-butanol (cosurfactant), toluene (oil phase), ferrocene (charge carrier) and various acids and bases (supporting electrolyte). We used cyclic voltammetry to study mass transport and reversibility parameters of the microemulsion system while varying the water to surfactant ratio and pH. The results obtained from the acidic and alkaline systems have CVs that show reversible behavior. Interestingly, the basic system exhibits a classic EC reaction at low scan rates likely producing dihydroxyferrocene. Unsurprisingly, at higher concentrations of acid or base the ester bond in the Tween is hydrolyzed, thus destroying the microemulsion system. While at intermediate pH values, however, the microemulsions are stable for extended periods of time.

title: Design Integration of Gasification and Reforming Technologies for Syngas Production
abstract: This study is focused on the production of syngas using gasification and dry methane reforming (DMR) technologies. The two processes are compared as a standalone design for a syngas production capacity of 10,000 kmol/h with H 2 to CO ratio of 0.88. The two processes are then integrated to develop a novel design that can reduce the CO 2 emissions to a near-zero level with reasonable amount of energy requirement. In this study, Aspen Plus® has been employed as a process simulation tool. The results reveal that the DMR process consumes 3.4 times less energy compared to a gasification plant of same capacity. The result also shows that the integration of gasification and DMR design off-sets the negative aspects of gasification technology enabling it to utilize conventional solid fossil fuel with low emission levels.

title: Hydrogen Rich Syngas Production through Biomass - Flare Gas Synergistic Co-Processing on Carbon Nanofiber (CNF) Based Catalyst
abstract: Researchers at West Virginia University have proposed a new reaction pathway focused towards process development of synergistic biomass – flare gas coprocessing to produce hydrogen rich syngas. The novelty of such a process is in-situ co-processing of waste natural gas (flare gas) and biomass along with CO 2 utilization to produce syngas with H 2 :CO = 2. Methane activated biomass gasification produces hydrogen rich syngas with >80 mole% H 2 in product gas. With addition of 1% CO 2 in the gas feed along with 5% CH 4 , synergistic methane – biomass – CO 2 reaction system produces controllable ratio of H 2 and CO based on the requirement downstream. New catalyst was developed with carbon nanofiber (CNF) support impregnated with iron (Fe) and molybdenum (Mo) for the natural gas – biomass gasification system. Fe-Mo/CNF catalyst offered dual functionality as Fe active sites caused CH 4 , CO 2 activation while Mo is highly active for deoxygenation of biomass oxygenates through strong oxygen binding. The deoxygenation of oxygen rich biomass provides steam adsorbates for steam reforming and dry reforming of CH 4 , CO 2 which produces hydrogen rich syngas. FeMo/CNF catalyst regeneration and reuse in multiple cycles was also investigated at temperatures 800, 850, and 900 o C. After 15 cycles of FeMo/CNF being subjected to reuse without external regeneration, it was observed that hydrogen rich syngas could be produced consistently with H 2 :CO ratio between 1.3 to 3.5. Interestingly, the CNF based catalyst undergoes self-regeneration after every 4 to 5 cycles evident from periodic rise and fall in the H 2 :CO ratio. Although the self-regeneration mechanism is not completely understood, it is evident from TEM imaging and XRD patterns of CNF catalyst subjected to 1, 5, 10, and 15 cycles. Multiple reuse of CNF without external regeneration causes shielding of nanofibers and nanotubes by coke but the metallic active sites were clearly visible for all the CNF samples under TEM. Carbon nanotube and fiber structures were visible and similar in the CNF catalyst samples subjected to 1 and 10 reuses. This indicates the catalyst undergoes self-regeneration to some extent. Self-regeneration of the catalyst may occur due to 3D coke formation leading to nanotube formation on the Fe active sites, as reported by Wang et al and Robinson et al. Hydrogen rich syngas production could be achieved by co-processing flare gas with biomass on-site along with CO 2 utilization on inexpensive CNF based catalyst synthesized in-house.

title: Investigating the Microstructural Effects of Electrode Compression on Redox Flow Battery Performance
abstract: Redox flow batteries (RFBs) promote the decarbonization of the electricity sector by enabling the storage of intermittent renewable energy over mid to long-duration timescales (hours-days). However, further cost reduction is necessary for ubiquitous adoption. Electrodes are particularly important components of the RFB system, and this study examines the effect of electrode compression on performance. Freudenberg paper and Avcarb cloth, common RFB electrodes with differing microstructures, were chosen for this study. We found that cloth electrodes elicited the highest surface area and electrochemical performance at 25% compression, whereas the carbon paper electrodes showed optimal performances at 10% compression. Additionally, the permeability of the cloth electrode increased at 10% compression compared to uncompressed material, but permeability decreased significantly at higher percentage compressions. We hypothesize that there exists a trade-off between porosity, permeability, and accessible surface area of the electrodes; this trade-off results in maximized performance at moderate compression of 25% and 10% for cloth and paper, respectively. Elucidating the relationship between compression, microstructure, and performance enables targeted electrode design that will optimize the performance and reduce costs of RFBs, promoting their utilization at the grid scale.

title: Experimental Evaluation of the Temperature Coefficient of Quinones' Redox Reactions
abstract: Due to their low cost, high abundance, and extensive tunability, organic redox couples, such as quinones, have become of high interest. Moreover, their wide range of redox potentials have recently become highly sought after in thermogalvanics, which describes the generation of a proportional electric potential when a temperature gradient is applied to electrochemical redox couples. With applications in low-powered electronics, quinones as thermogalvanics have shown great potential in waste heat harvesting. The main objectives of this study were to manufacture a prototype setup that would record the hot and cold temperature, and the open-circuit voltage of an electrochemical reaction, leading to the evaluation of the non-isothermal temperature coefficient (α) of the reaction; and to determine the α value of different quinone redox reactions at different pH levels in aqueous solution. The redox reaction between p-benzoquinone and p-hydroquinone was successfully studied in unbuffered and buffered acidic media with ∂E/∂T ranging from -0.32 to -1.02 mV/K. Although data showed hysteresis, at a pH of 10, ∂E/∂T was -2.07 mV/K, surpassing the ferri/ferrocyanide α value of -1.4 mV/K, which is considered the highest temperature coefficient recorded. Experimental values demonstrated a linear fit as per the Nernst equation. Moreover, electrochemical oxidation of p-hydroquinone above neutral pH resulted in irreversible reactions producing anionic species of p-benzoquinone.

title: Optimization of Graphene/Mn 3 O 4 active Layer and Gel Polymer Electrolyte of All-Printed Supercapacitor for Space Applications
abstract: Energy storage is essential for space exploration, communication, and operation of electrical systems beyond Earth’s orbit. Due to the inherent variability of renewables, reliable energy storage devices are necessary to make future renewable energy sources viable. The most common form of energy storage is the battery, because of its high energy density, but the battery lacks the superior specific power as well as high cyclic durability required for fast energy transfer as in a capacitor. A supercapacitor is an energy storage device which implements the best of batteries and capacitors, ultimately identifying a device with high specific energy and specific power, and robust cyclic durability . A key project of space energy storage is In Space Manufacturing (ISM). ISM furthers advancement of space technology by allowing for complete fabrication of devices in space, reducing the cost and energy required to transport materials to target locations such as the International Space Station, Moon or Mars . Supercapacitor technology in space is important for triboelectric energy harvesting and solar harvesting; variability of wind and solar sources requires storage in a reliable device. The crucial features determining performance of a supercapacitor are the active layer and the electrolyte layer. This study focuses on optimizing not only these essential layers, but also the extrusion printing technique. Success if determined by analyzing cyclic durability and printing stability. The studied supercapacitor utilizes a silver current collector layer, a graphene active layer, and a lithium-chloride gel polymer electrolyte. This research can be implemented further with analysis on radiation effects of the 3-D printed supercapacitor and future optimization of the active layer including research into non-binder inks.

title: Co-Solvent Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Wastewater Algae
abstract: Decreasing supplies of non-renewable fuels create demand for a new and renewable source of transportation fuels. Algal biomass harvested from wastewater treatment plants has the potential to fulfill this need due to its abundance and suitability for conversion into fuels. Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), a thermochemical conversion process in which biomass is heated in a pressurized liquid, can be used to generate products with energy contents higher than that of the original feedstock. HTL of algae produces liquid bio-crude oil, which can be upgraded into a liquid fuel, as well as residual char and aqueous phase which can be used for nutrient recovery and reuse. Alcohol co-solvents have been shown to increase the yield and quality of bio-crude oil from HTL of algae. Here, ethanol, isopropanol, and glycerol were tested as HTL co-solvents using a 1.8 L Parr reactor at different operating temperatures and residence times. Glycerol produced the highest yield of desired products compared to the other alcohols. Crude glycerol, which contains residual methanol and fatty acids, is a byproduct biodiesel production. Using crude glycerol in HTL of algae creates a value-added use for two low-value process streams. Co-solvent HTL products were characterized using bomb calorimetry, CHNS elemental analysis, and Fourier transform mass spectroscopy.

title: Waste Plastic Generation Profile of Kampala, Uganda
abstract: Pollution is a significant global challenge. Municipal solid waste accumulates on land due to many reasons. In some rural areas, waste management solutions are nonexistent, meaning waste piles around residential locations. One sustainable solution to this problem considers the complete elimination of plastic from the ecosystem, unlike many other current methods. While methods such as recycling are great for reusing plastic already produced, it can only be used so much before it ends back in the waste pile. Instead, by creating another purpose for this waste plastic, there will be a lot less plastic that ends up in the environment and buried underneath the ground. This solution is termed as Trash to Tank (3T), a process that converts waste plastic types (polystyrene, polypropylene, low-density polyethylene, and high-density polyethylene) into Plastic Derived Fuel Oil (PDFO) via pyrolysis. Pyrolysis is a method of thermal decomposition that occurs in the absence of oxygen while burning. The fuel produced is similar in composition to diesel and kerosene. Uganda is a suitable country for the use of 3T method because it lacks sufficient capital and infrastructure to manage all of its waste. In order to optimize the utilization of 3T process, reduce waste plastic accumulation on land and in the natural waterways of Uganda (River Nile and Lake Victoria), a waste plastic generation profile must be developed and analyzed. This study accomplishes this for a small subset of Uganda, Kampala, the capital city. Through a partnership with Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA), a local waste management municipality, existent waste plastic generation was determined for the city. This information was correlated with available data on population density and geographical analysis of income level via ArcGIS (a spatial analysis tool) to understand the impact of population and income on waste generation. The results of this study reveal the interplay of these factors for waste plastic management in Kampala and similar sub-Saharan African cities.

title: The Effects of pH and Complexation on Metal Cation Uptake in Nanoparticle Organic Hybrid Material (NOHM) Systems
abstract: The potential use of nanoparticle organic hybrid materials (NOHM) as electrolytes in redox flow batteries is being explored. Redox flow batteries present the advantage of providing large-scale energy storage, beyond the capacity of more common battery types. The most common active material used is currently Vanadium, which is expensive in a pure form, has a corrosive environment, and decreases battery capacity over time. NOHMs are composite particles formed by polymers grafted (either ionically or covalently) onto surface-modified inorganic nanoparticles. Such structure has great potential to capture and carry nonpolar electroactive species. A NOHM comprised of a silica core ionically grafted with polyethylenimine (PEI) polymers is focused on in this study, we refer to this as NOHM-I-PEI. Copper is introduced as a probe to evaluate the effect NOHM structures have on metal cation uptake. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was used to investigate the electrochemical behavior of the copper species as the concentration of NOHM increases at a fixed Cu(NO 3 ) 2 concentration. NOHM-I-PEI showed inhibition of the oxidation and reduction peaks as the NOHM concentration increased, suggesting the formation of the cuprammonium complex. UV-Vis measurements also suggested the presence of this complex. pH measurements taken for each solution shoed a drastic change along the range of solutions tested. The pH of the solutions was controlled via Britton-Robinson buffers and CVs were ran with this set of solutions. Results from testing these solutions allow for better isolation of the NOHM’s effect from the effect of pH. It is observed that peak intensity decreases as the pH increases. At high pH (>6) complete inhibition is observed, while at lower pH, two cathodic peaks can be seen. Based on these results, it is hypothesized that the bound copper is not available for oxidation/reduction at high pH. Whereas at lower pH, the observed variation in intensity can be related to complexation as a function of the nitrogen to copper ratio. The presence of two cathodic peaks can be explained by the stabilization of the cuprous ion due to complexation.

title: Permselective Separators for Grid Storage Alkaline Zn/MnO 2 Batteries
abstract: Increasing awareness of climate change and the dangers of fossil fuels have spurred a need for faster integration of renewable energy sources onto the electrical grid. Rechargeable alkaline Zn/MnO 2 batteries have emerged as a candidate to fill this need as they are low-cost, possess a high energy density, are environmentally inert, and can be readily mass produced [1]. A layered Bi-birnessite oxide with Cu 2+ intercalation has recently been developed that stabilizes the MnO 2 structure and allows continuous cycling at near full 2e- capacity [2]. However, one of the technical hurdles is overcoming limited cycle life caused by the formation of irreversible and resistive ZnMn 2 O 4 and ZnO species on the cathode when zincate ([Zn(OH) 4 ] 2- ) diffuses across the battery separators [3]. In this presentation, we demonstrate the use of new permselective polymeric separators that can be used in high depth of discharge Zn/MnO 2 batteries. Several separators were screened for their zincate blocking abilities using our recently developed anodic stripping voltammetry methodology [4]. The polymeric separators were also tested for hydroxide diffusion where it is shown that they demonstrate selectivity for the monovalent hydroxide anion. A primary discharge of the full 2e - capacity of MnO 2 (617 mA h g -1 ) was used to further test the ionic selectivity of the separators where the 2 nd e - discharge plateau, indicative of the absence of zinc, was observed only for Zn/MnO 2 batteries that utilized the selective polymeric separators. title: Thermal Conductivity of Ionic Liquids and Hydrofluorocarbons: 1-Hexyl-3-Methyl-Imidazolium Bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)Amide and 1,1,1,2-Tetrafluoroethane
abstract: Novel vapor absorption refrigeration processes utilizing ionic liquids (ILs) and the hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant gas, 1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane (R-134a) have been recently investigated. The low volatility of ionic liquids allows them to be used as ideal solvents in such processes with no need for bulky rectifying columns to purify the refrigerant of residual solvent. Employing the use of ILs in vapor absorption refrigeration cycles paves way for more efficient energy usage. Transport properties of such mixtures are needed for further design processes. The IL, 1-hexyl-3-methyl-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)amide ([HMim][Tf 2 N]) was investigated as a model solvent. In this study, liquid thermal conductivities of [HMim][Tf 2 N] saturated with R-134a at 25 ⁰C, 50 ⁰C, and 75 ⁰C with pressures ranging from 0.7 bar to 18.9 bar were measured. Herein, a transient hot wire method was used to determine that the values of the thermal conductivity of pure [HMim][Tf 2 N] were in good agreement with those reported in the literature. The ionic liquid and R-134a mixture values show a trend of decreasing thermal conductivities with increased refrigerant solubility compared to those values obtained for pure [HMim][Tf 2 N]. Trends in thermal conductivity change based on composition of R-134a in [HMim][Tf 2 N] have provided compelling evidence that the effects of [HMim][Tf 2 N] on thermal conductivity are greater than those of R-134a.

title: Development of a Simplified Combustion Kinetic Model for Autothermal Biomass Pyrolysis
abstract: A simplified combustion kinetic model was developed to assess the autothermal operation of a biomass fast pyrolysis reactor. For that, single- and two-step combustion mechanisms of Westbrook and Dryer (1981) [Ref 1] were reviewed, coded using Aspen Plus and then validated with the detailed kinetic model provided by Chemkin for hydrocarbons and alcohols. Artificial intelligence tools were further used to predict the values of important kinetic rate constants associated with the simplified model for fuel chemicals generated in the biomass fast pyrolysis reactor. The two-step combustion mechanism model qualitatively describes fuel combustion patterns for hydrocarbons once the fuel is ignited, although it does not simulate chemical ignition delay during which the fuel undergoes radical decomposition before actually starting the oxidation reaction. Machine Learning algorithms prove quite satisfactory in correlating the kinetic parameters for the combustion of alkanes but fail to assertively calculate them for oxygenated molecules due to the lack of such data points in training set. Future work involves the refinement of the two-step combustion mechanism for oxygenated fuels and the improvement of the machine learning features to achieve robust prediction for the rate constants associated with oxygenated molecules. References Ref 1: CK Westbrook and FL Dryer, "Simplified Reaction Mechanisms for the Oxidation of Hydrocarbon Fuels in Flames," Combustion Science and Technology (1981) 27:31-43.

title: An Ultrafast Rechargeable Aluminum Battery
abstract: Demand for electric vehicles is rising due to environmental concerns, government subsidies, and improved battery performance. Lithium ion batteries may not be able to scale with the increasing demand due to their limited amount of stored charge, long re-charging times, high cost and risk of fire. Aluminum batteries are a promising replacement for lithium-ion batteries not only because aluminum is much more abundant and less expensive than lithium, but because aluminum batteries are non-flammable, have 4x the volumetric charge capacity of lithium ion batteries, and have ultrafast recharging capabilities. The focus of this research was creating an ultrafast, safe, cheap and long-cycling-life rechargeable aluminum battery for electric vehicles. The prototype batteries are composed of an aluminum-indium anode, a selenium cathode, and a molten salt (NaCl-KCl-AlCl 3 ) electrolyte. While lithium ion batteries, have a charging rate of about 1.0 C, our aluminum batteries reach a rate of 200 C (18 seconds) due to the molten salt promoting a high power. Our aluminum batteries demonstrated excellent rate performance, high coulombic efficiency (~90%) and good stability during early testing. Our prototypes are a promising energy storage alternative that could help to propel the electric vehicle industry forward with safe, affordable, high capacity and fast re-charging batteries.

title: Light Weight Plasticized Concrete - an Evolution of Sustaining Sustainability.
abstract: Recently, a warning was issued by the UN quoting “World nearing critical point of no return” by 2030 and further debates on sustainable development. Plastic warms the earth twice as much as aviation. Also, plastics are not only polluting but also, they make climate change worse. The most versatile man-made product used in the world is concrete. Concrete uses mainly natural resources like sand, coarse aggregate and fine aggregate, thus depleting these resources exponentially. So, to overcome these major issues we made “SLWP concrete” (The Sustainable Light Weight Plastic concrete). The natural resources like fine and coarse aggregate used in concrete were replaced by 3rd grade waste plastic like HDPE, LDPE, PP, PET in three different variations such as, first replacing coarse aggregate by waste plastic moulds of size 20mm down in two batches (i.e. 50% and 100% by volume). Then, secondly by replacing fine aggregate by waste plastic beads 4.75mm down in again two batches (i.e.50% and 100% by volume) and replacing both fine and coarse aggregate with same combinations. The compressive strength of SLWP concrete showed an increase in strength by 10% and 40% after 7 days and 28 days respectively compared to that of conventional concrete when coarse aggregate was fully replaced. Similar results were obtained when the experiment was repeated with batches of coarse aggregate and fine aggregate too. The results also reveals that of 10%-30% decrease in weight has been observed in SLWP concrete w.r.t conventional concrete. Also, SLWP concrete is economical due to replacement of natural resources by waste plastic. This model was developed with multiple variations to conserve natural treasure and expel the haphazard plastic waste. This method of recovering plastic helps to restore balance in the Eco cycle and to maintain sustainability.

title: Development of a Flow-Free Gradient Generator Using a Thiol-Acrylate Microfluidic Resin/Hydrogel (TAMR/H) Hybrid System
abstract: Microfluidic gradient generators have been used to study the migration, growth, and drug response of numerous biological systems including cancer cells and algae. Traditional approaches using serpentine channels produce highly stable gradients; however, these devices require direct flow over the cells, which limits their compatibility with suspension cultures. Flow-free gradient generators have been utilized, but they are often hindered by the need for negative flow or external clamps to maintain fluid-tight seals between the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and hydrogel. The goal of this work was to develop new polymeric materials using thiol-acrylate chemistry to produce a two-layer, flow-free microfluidic gradient generator capable of rapid and facile bonding to maintain fluid-tight channels. The geometry of the device consisted of three parallel channels where a chemoattractant or chemorepellent was flowed through the outermost channel to create a chemical gradient within the center ‘flow-free’ channel. The fluidic channels were imprinted into a rigid top layer, fabricated using thiol-acrylate microfluidic resin (TAMR). The TAMR was bound to a thiol-acrylate hydrogel (H), which served as the bottom layer of the device, and allowed for the flow-free diffusion of chemicals between three parallel channels. The TAMR/H hybrid device consisted of activated acrylate resin made by covalently bonding an amine-curing agent into the acrylate resin coupled with a thiol-containing reagent that is thoroughly mixed into the resin. The hydrogel consists of thiol and acrylate groups within an aqueous buffer. The diffusion of biomolecules through the TAMR/H system and development of a stable chemical gradient was confirmed both experimentally using fluorescent microscopy and computationally using COMSOL. The stability, stiffness, and adhesive strength of the TAMR/H device was thoroughly characterized to confirm proper device operation. The performance of the TAMR/H device was compared to a control PDMS/agarose device with a similar geometry. As proof of concept, the TAMR/H microfluidic device was used to study the chemotactic response of a highly motile strain of GFP-expressing Escherichia coli . The migratory response of both wild type and mutant E. coli was observed in both the TAMR/H and PDMS/agarose microfluidic devices. Population-based analysis confirmed a similarity in performance between the two materials verifying that TAMR/H was a viable alternative to PDMS-based microfluidic devices. These findings highlight the utility of the TAMR/H hybrid system, which has the potential to perform a suite of experiments spanning 3D cell migration and dynamic co-culture between different cell types commonly found in heterogeneous environments like biofilms and cancer.
