title: Development and Modeling of Cu@Ag Core-Shell Nanoparticle Catalysts with Galvanic Replacement for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
abstract: Efficient solar-driven electrochemical CO 2 reduction (CO 2 RR) would provide a carbon-neutral source of fuels and chemical precursors. Copper (Cu) is a catalyst that has been widely studied for CO 2 RR due to its moderate CO binding strength and the variety of products it is able to catalyze. Recent advances in CO 2 RR have made use of engineered nanoscale catalysts with various sizes and morphologies of Cu nanoparticles. One of the main goals of CO 2 RR is shifting selectivity towards C 2+ products, which have higher energy densities and are more profitable when compared to other products. While a Cu catalyst alone produces mostly hydrogen and hydrocarbon products, introducing other metals at the interface changes the interaction between reaction intermediates and surface atoms, enabling tuning of the selectivity. For example, the introduction of silver (Ag) allows for a synergistic effect during catalysis that leads to a shift in selectivity towards oxygenated products, which are not observed with either Cu or Ag separately. Additionally, core-shell bimetallic nanoparticles allow the two metals to be present in close proximity instead of a physical mixture of monometallic particles. Furthermore, the distribution of the two metals can be reliably tuned via a galvanic replacement reaction (GRR). In this work, we present a colloidal synthesis of Cu-Ag bimetallic nanoparticles, employing GRR to precisely control the shell thickness with a diffusion-based self-limiting mechanism. Using Cu-Ag as an example system, we develop a mathematical model based on transport, diffusion, and surface energies that describes the formation of the Ag shell on a Cu core and explains the self-limiting nature of the reaction. The nanoparticles are characterized with bulk composition measurements like ICP-OES and elemental mapping with STEM-EDS to analyze the shell thickness as a function of several reaction parameters. The synthesis demonstrates highly uniform particles with controlled shell thicknesses where colloidal stability is maintained, an important consideration for uniformity when covering the surface of an electrode. The results of the characterization are compared with the model and demonstrate good agreement with experimental results. Since our mathematical model depends only physical material constants, it may be applied to various bimetallic systems to engineer the next generation of nanoscale catalysts and further enhance the selectivity of the CO 2 RR towards desired products.

title: Dynamics of Graphene Sheets at a Water-Vapor Interface: A Molecular Dynamics Study
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of particles at fluid-fluid interfaces has attracted considerable research interest over the past several decades as fluid interfaces create an environment where monolayer thin films can be assembled through a ‘bottom-up’ approach. For example, fluid-fluid interfaces have been used to manufacture highly transparent and electrically conductive thin films of graphene flakes as it has been shown that graphene flakes are thermodynamically favorable at the interface between two immiscible fluids. However, the dynamics of film formation and the interactions between graphene flakes are currently not understood. Furthermore, it has proven difficult to isolate and experimentally probe the dynamics of pristine monolayer graphene flakes at fluid-fluid interfaces. This study aims to address this gap by using computational simulations, which have been shown to reliably estimate real-world experimental scenarios. Molecular dynamics simulations were employed to investigate the lateral interactions and stacking dynamics of mono- and few-layer graphene flakes at a vapor-water interface. Adaptive biasing force (ABF) simulations were used to render potential of mean force profiles and identify different stacking pathways. Additionally, distance versus time profiles were generated for two interacting monolayer flakes and the results were fit according to a power law relation to understand how the interaction pair potential scaled with center-to-center separation distance. Ultimately, this study offers a new perspective into the investigation of interactions between interfacially-bound particles.

title: Rheology & Thermal Stability of Supercritical CO 2 foams at Different Temperatures and SDS Concentrations
abstract: The use of nanoparticles (NP) combined with surfactants has been a novel practice in the generation of CO 2 foams for hydraulic fracturing. This combination reduces water consumption and formation damage, while improving apparent viscosity and stability of the generated foam. This study evaluates the synergistic effects between nanoparticles and surfactants in CO 2 foams and how surfactant concentration affects the rheology and stability of the CO 2 foam. To assess the rheology and stability of CO 2 foam, nanoparticle dispersion with surfactant is co-injected with high pressure CO 2 at 1500 psi in the CO 2 accumulator and 1300 psi at the system outlet through a bead pack at different temperatures. The generated foam flows through a capillary tube and the pressure drop along the tube is used to calculate the foam apparent viscosity. The heights and texture of the generated foam in the sapphire tube is recorded over time to assess foam stability. To assess the effects of surfactant concentration, the temperature in the chamber is fixed and the concentration of surfactant is changed. To assess the effects of temperature, the surfactant concentration is fixed, and the temperature is changed. From the results, the mixture of nanoparticles and surfactant offered stronger and more viscous foams as compared to foams generated with nanoparticles alone. This is attributed to the synergistic effects between nanoparticles and surfactants, which is believed to form a steric barrier comprised of nanoparticles and enhanced with surfactants at the water/CO 2 interface. The structural integrity reduces the film drainage, the interfacial tension, and film coalescence, which contribute to higher foam performance. The combination of surfactant with nanoparticles in foam generation can offer enhanced foam stability and foam apparent viscosity, which helps maintain foam properties and provide better proppant transport under harsh reservoir conditions.

title: Synthesizing and Modeling the Optical Properties of Silica Aerogel
abstract: The purpose of this project is to model the optical properties of silica aerogel by solving the 1-D radiative transfer equation (RTE). Silica aerogel is an optically transparent and thermally insulative material with a very low density. Due to its microstructure, which consists of a thing solid backbone of silica particle aggregates enveloping thousands of nanoscopic pores, the material suppresses the three modes of heat transfer. The unique combination of physical and chemical properties allows silica aerogel to be an excellent candidate for solar thermal energy applications. The forward solution to the 1-D RTE will predict the transmittance and reflectance of the aerogel as functions of both scattering albedo and extinction, which are inherent properties of the material. By compiling the numerical results of the forward solution, separate 2-D contour plots can be constructed wherein scattering albedo is plotted versus optical thickness, and the contour gradient represents the theoretical transmittance and reflectance. To determine the intrinsic properties of a specific sample, the transmittance and reflectance of that particular sample must first be determined experimentally using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer equipped with an integrating sphere to account for losses. Once values for transmittance and reflectance are available, the values may be plotted as single contour lines on the previously constructed contour plots which constitute the backward solution to the RTE. When these two plots are superimposed upon one another, it is found that the curves intersect at exactly one data point. This solution point provides the exact scattering albedo and extinction coefficient for a specific sample of silica aerogel. Repeating this process for several samples of aerogel produced by various synthesis processes and with different thicknesses will allow the team to predict the transmittance of a sample synthesized by a specific procedure and of a particular thickness. Furthermore, obtaining the intrinsic properties of a sample will allow for the calculation of the scattering coefficient of that sample, which can be used to determine the approximate pore diameter of the sample. The calculated pore diameter will be verified using Small-Angle X-Ray Scattering. Since the pore size of the resulting aerogel directly affects the degree to which light is scattered throughout the medium, it would be useful to predict the transmittance of a sample characterized by a certain pore size and vice versa; this will indeed be possible using the model formulated in this project.

title: Peptoid-Functionalized Gold Nanoparticles for Use in Electrochemical Sensors
abstract: Detection of pathogenic organisms is a key part of providing medical care to global communities. Current detection methods are slow, expensive, and sometimes unable to provide the sensitivity and specificity necessary for accurate measurements and effective treatment plans. Electrochemical sensors enhanced with peptoid-functionalized nanoparticles are an alternative to traditional techniques that offers rapid, accurate detection of pathogens. These sensors work by undergoing an electrochemical reaction when their electrodes come into contact with a target molecule; peptoid-functionalized nanoparticle electrode coatings have the potential to increase the speed and specificity of these reactions. Preparation of these modified gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) involves the exchange of stabilizing molecules added during AuNP synthesis for thiol-terminating peptoids designed to provide desired functionality. This surface modification procedure is complicated by both aggregation of AuNPs in peptoid-containing solution and adsorption of peptoid-functionalized AuNPs to polypropylene centrifuge tubes. Successful implementation of functionalized AuNPs in this project requires that no aggregation occurs to limit the functionality of the peptoid or AuNP. Multiple peptoids were observed to cause AuNP aggregation and adsorption, with aggregation rates proportional to the concentration of added peptoid; changes were monitored via visual observation of solution color and solution absorbance measurements. To attempt to delay or eliminate aggregation, solutions were reacted in a variety of different conditions, including the presence of sodium hydroxide or Tween 20, refrigeration, incubation, mixing, and absence of light. Alternatives to an aqueous solution, such as phosphate buffer solution (PBS), were also tested. The identification of a method to stabilize the AuNPs during the peptoid functionalization process is essential to future work on the binding capabilities of peptoid-functionalized AuNPs with proteins found on the surface of pathogenic viruses.

title: Effect of Functional Groups on the Adsorption of Lighthydrocarbons in Fmj -Type Metal−Organic Frameworks
abstract: Adsorption is considered to be an effective method of light hydrocarbon storage which has advantages in safety and efficiency. Metal − organic frameworks (MOF) , a group of crystalline porous materials with periodic network structure assembled from coordination bond by metal ions/clusters and organic ligands, are considered as promising candidates for light hydrocarbons adsorption due to their highly regulated channel and modified skeleton.The functionalized modification of targeted porous metal − organic frameworks (MOFs) is important to improve the adsorption capacity of light hydrocarbon gases. In this study, five isomorphic MOFs with different functional groups (F,Cl, NH 2 , CH 3 , and OCH 3 ) are successfully synthesized by systematic functional modification of UMCM-151. By studying the adsorption properties of C2 and C3 hydrocarbons (C 2 H 2 , C 2 H 4 , C 2 H 6 , C 3 H 6 , and C 3 H 8 ), it is found that the electron-withdrawing group functional UMCM-151-F and UMCM-151-Cl exhibit strong affinity for C 2 H 2 (98.71 cm 3 g − 1 for UMCM-151-F and 90.29 cm 3 g − 1 for UMCM-151-Cl), while the electron-donating group functional UMCM-151-NH 2 , UMCM-151-CH 3 , and UMCM-151-OCH 3 have strong affinity for C 2 H 4 (97.89 cm 3 g − 1 for UMCM-151-NH 2 , 90.22 cm 3 g − 1 for UMCM-151-CH 3 and 94.13 cm 3 g − 1 for UMCM-151-OCH 3 ). The differences in affinity of electron effects for light hydrocarbon provide an experimental basis for porous MOFs to improve their light hydrocarbon storage capacity.

title: Evaluating the Fluid and Aerodynamic Properties of Uio-66 Nanoparticles
abstract: Pulmonary diseases such as lung cancer, cystic fibrosis, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD) are associated with alarming annual mortality and morbidity rates [1]. Evidently, current therapies for pulmonary diseases are inadequate, and the seriousness of many pulmonary diseases motivates a need for improved pulmonary drug delivery [2]. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), coordination compounds of metals and ligands, offer promise as nanoparticle drug delivery vehicles due to their cargo-loading capacity, tunable pore size, and potential biocompatibility [3]. The goal of this project is to evaluate relevant fluid and aerodynamic properties of a specific zirconium-based MOF, UiO-66, for drug delivery applications. The cargo-loading, fluid and aerodynamic properties were characterized, while the biocompatibility was confirmed. UiO-66 particles were synthesized under acid-free conditions, with water content, synthesis time, and ligand:metal ratio controlled to modulate the particle size. Using a fluorescent assay, the cargo-loading was characterized for a model cargo, rhodamine B (RB) using particles with varying amounts structural defects, or defectiveness. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) was utilized to measure the hydrodynamic diameter (ZAVG) of particles. The aerodynamic diameter of the particles was characterized using a next generation impactor (NGI), after particles were aerosolized using a collision jet nebulizer. Finally, cytotoxicity was analyzed through a cell titer glow assay after dosing murine-derived alveolar macrophages (MH-S) with particles. The results of SEM yielded geometric radii between 30-120 nm. The median mass aerodynamic diameter (MMAD) decreased from 0.64 μm for unloaded particles to 0.42 μm for max-loaded particles at 7.63% defectiveness. At all other defectiveness levels, a similar decrease was observed. The ZAVG diameter consistently decreased as loading increased across all defectiveness levels. Finally, after dosing alveolar macrophages, no acute toxicity or inflammatory response was observed. The observed decrease in MMAD for loaded particles is an important result, as generational pulmonary deposition depends primarily on aerodynamic particle size. The lack of acute cell immune response after dosage also supports the viability of UiO-66 as pulmonary drug delivery vehicles. References: [1] The top 10 causes of death, Fact sheet N°310. title: Formation of Poly(ethylene glycol) Coatings on Silicon Surfaces Via Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions
abstract: Attachment of 4-vinylbenzyl chloride (VBC) monolayers to hydrogen-terminated silicon through UV-induced hydrosilylation generates a surface coating (g-VBC) that can be further modified via substitution reactions at the benzyl chloride moiety. To apply g-VBC in synthesizing functional coatings, we demonstrated the attachment of poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether 2000 (PEG2000) via nucleophilic substitution. Two reaction systems were used to produce PEG-modified silicon substrates. In the first approach, the deprotonated hydroxyl end of PEG2000 was reacted with surface bound benzyl chloride sites. A variety of reaction conditions were compared to determine those most conducive to high conversion at the surface. In a second approach, VBC was reacted with PEG2000 in solution, and the resulting compound was then grafted to hydrogen-terminated silicon via UV-induced hydrosilylation. For both of these approaches, characterization methods included contact angle measurements to assess wetting and ellipsometry to determine surface thickness. The fouling resistance of the PEG-modified substrates were compared using a FITC-albumin assay to test for non-specific protein adsorption. The developed reaction schemes are of particular interest as they yield Si – C bound films expected to exhibit greater hydrolytic stability than alkoxysilane- and chlorosilane-based methods reliant on siloxane bonds to attach coatings on silicon.

title: Run-to-Run Reproducibility in Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy
abstract: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a powerful method that can be used to detect analyte interactions on the surface of the working electrode. However, reproducibility issues associated with a repeated impedance measurements of similar conditions using EIS is known. 1 We have identified methodology that can be used to improve the reproducibility of repeated EIS impedance measurements. Multiple factors were taken into consideration for run to run measurement variation such as buffer solution concentration ( e.g. 20mM vs 1 mM ferri/ferrocyanide as a redox couple), buffer solution composition ( e.g. phosphate buffer solution vs. deionized water), and EIS setup options ( e.g. DC offset conditions and N 2 purging). Additionally, techniques such as removing electrodes and rinsing them were tested ( i.e. the working, auxiliary, and reference electrodes were removed and rinsed in between EIS measurements). Some techniques were found to hinder or not affect EIS measurement reproducibility, while others supported reproducible measurements. Taking these methods into account, the most reproducible model of repeated EIS impedance measurements will be discussed. title: Layer-By-Layer Films of Photosystem I and Conducting Polymers
abstract: The integration of Photosystem I (PSI), an essential protein in photosynthesis, into photoelectrochemical cells for environmentally sustainable solar energy conversion has gained attention recently because of the protein’s nearly perfect quantum yield, vast abundance, and nanoscale size. My research examines PSI’s capability to form organic thin films with electrically conducting polymer interlayers. This strategy allows for parts of the polymer to extend into the PSI structure and act as an electron transfer medium between the electrode and protein or between protein layers. I form these films using layer-by-layer (LBL) Deposition, where each molecular layer on the electrode is electrostatically attached to each other by alternating charge. In this case, a layer of PSI containing mixed charge is alternated with a layer of the mixed-charged conducting polymer PEDOT:PSS for up to 10 layer pairs. Film thickness increases by an average of 1.9 nm per polymer layer and 6.2 nm per PSI layer. Infrared spectra are consistent with the presence of both the protein as well as both parts of the PEDOT:PSS polymer in the film. Contact angles were used to assess the composition of the outermost surface of the film after each deposition. Changes in contact angle are consistent with distinct layers adding to the total film for up to ten total layer pairs. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy shows that the polymer entraps ions well to provide minimal change in impedance with increasing film thickness. Finally, photochronoamperometry shows that the photocurrent of the layered films on an electrode increases up to a critical number of layer pairs.

title: Development of IL Based Low-Temperature Electrolyte for MET Siesmometer Utilizing Molecular Interactions
abstract: Room temperature ionic liquids (IL), cation-anion pairs that remain liquid at room temperature, have proven to function effectively as electrolytes in a variety of applications, including energy storage devices and sensors. Several unique traits allow for IL to broaden the operating temperature window of the electrolyte. Among these are its wide liquidus range, low volatility, and good thermal and electrochemical stability. The strategy of incorporating other solvents or salts with ILs is broadly applied for enhancements on critical physicochemical properties of an electrolyte. In particular, IL based systems show tremendous potential as electrolytes for the molecular electronic transducer (MET) seismometer to conduct seismology studies under harsh environments. In this work, we present a system consisting of IL, organic solvents, and salt, specifically designed for MET sensing technology at ultra-low temperatures. We discovered that through the formation of hydrogen bonds between the imidazolium cation and the organic solvents, the coulombic attractions between cations and anions are weakened, as evidenced by NMR spectrums. Furthermore, the molar ratio of components in the system has been tuned to optimize the molecular interactions, where neither organic solvent caused undesired first-order phase transitions. This tuned electrolyte boasted a glass transition temperature (T g ) at -119 ˚C, marking the lower temperature working limit of the system. Additionally, experimental results confirmed improvements in fluidity and ionic conductivity over the temperature range of 25 to -75 ˚C when compared to a previously developed aqueous based electrolyte system. Furthermore, the electrochemical stability of the proposed electrolyte is validated to be compatible with the MET sensing technology. Knowledge of the presented work may support the operation of MET seismometers and provide insights for future developments of low-temperature IL based electrolytes.

title: Immobilization of Laccase on Plantain Fibers for Dye Degradation
abstract: Immobilization process is a commonly used method involving a support used as a structural component and a catalytic component to maximize the properties of both elements and increase the application range. This is a common technique for generation of heterogeneous catalysts. Characteristics of a competitive support for catalyst are affinity, availability and low-cost. In this study, fibers extracted from pseudostem plantain (waste produced by plantain harvests) were used as support for commercial laccase immobilization by adsorption process. Mechanical and enzymatic pretreatments were made to modificate morphology of fiber surface or its superficial area. Laccase adsorption was evaluated through remaining enzymatic activity on fiber, and characterization assays as SEM, FTIR and electrokinetic properties were studied to examine the structural modifications on material surface. Process parameters used during the immobilization (Temperature, contact time and pH value) were analyzed in terms of indigo carmine dye degradation. The change of absorbance was evaluated by UV-Vis. The results showed that a 98 % of degradation was observed after 2 h using immobilized laccase at basic pH values and 5°C of storage temperature. Thus, the immobilization of commercial laccase on plantain fibers is an available strategy for production of low-cost, and functional catalyst for textile industries.

title: The Effect of Short‐Range Attractions on Sequence‐Defined Polyelectrolyte
abstract: Complex coacervation is the liquid-liquid phase separation of polyelectrolytes in aqueous salt solution into a polymer-dense phase, the coacervate, and a polymer-dilute phase, the supernatant. Previous work using Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that changing the sequence of charged and neutral monomers on polyelectrolytes while keeping the charge fraction constant alters the extent of phase separation. However, previous data does not account for the hydrophobicity of different neutral monomers. To understand the coacervation of polymers with various chemical structures, van der Waals interactions at various strengths are included in Monte Carlo simulations to show hydrophobic effects in the system. Comparisons are made to existing Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data. Understanding these patterning effects will enhance the knowledge of biomacromolecule phase separation, as well as expand the understanding of sequence-dependent polymer physics.

title: Predicting Polyelectrolyte-Micelle Phase Transitions: A Study in Charge Densities
abstract: In solution, electrostatic complexation may drive oppositely-charged macro-ions to undergo associative phase separation into a complex coacervate phase – a dense, polyelectrolyte-rich liquid with widespread applications across a range of industries — and a dilute phase, the supernatant. The widespread applications of coacervates for molecular separation and controlled delivery have resulted in extensive analysis of the phase behavior and properties of polyelectrolyte-micelle systems. However, much of the work to date has focused primarily on the effects of micellar surface charge density with model polymer-surfactant complexes. Thus, our objective is to explore the effects of stoichiometry and micellar chemistry over a larger phase space, with the goal of constructing a predictive framework for polyelectrolyte-micelle phase separation based on species’ charge densities. Here, we utilize a combination of turbidimetry coupled with optical microscopy to characterize the phase behavior of complexes between the cationic polymer poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) with surfactant micelles containing a mixture of the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and the neutral surfactant Triton X-100 (TX100) as a function of composition and salt concentration. Morphology mapping of coacervate formation will help inform future experiments focusing on understanding the effects of both micelle chemistry and polymer charge density. The results from this study will broaden the array of polyelectrolyte-micelle systems for applications such as biomolecular encapsulation and drug delivery.

title: Thermal Stabilization of Invasion Plasmid Antigen D (IpaD) Using Silica Gels
abstract: The structure of vaccine proteins is vital to maintaining vaccine effectivity; however, exposure to heat can disrupt intermolecular interactions maintaining the secondary and tertiary structures of proteins, thereby making the vaccine ineffective. The cold chain is the system of maintaining vaccine potency by transporting them at constant 2-8°C environment. Unfortunately, it is estimated that 50% of vaccines are wasted before use due to breaks in the cold chain, according to the World Health Organization. Many preservation methods have been applied including entrapment (via sol-gel matrix), adsorption, and covalent attachment. Of these, adsorption has the simplest chemical procedure and does not require harsh chemicals. Silica is often used as an adsorbent due to its porosity, hydrophilic properties, and high thermal stability. Silica is also used in nature to protect organisms from heat denaturation. For example, small organisms such as diatoms and radiolaria are known to wrap themselves in a silica coating for heat protection. Due to these properties, silica has high potential to biomimetically protect and preserve vaccine proteins during transport. Here, we examine the adsorption of Invasion Plasmid Antigen D (IpaD) onto various mesoporous silica gels and study the protein’s increased thermal stability on these solid supports for creating a cold chain independent vaccine. The solution depletion method using UV-Vis is utilized to study the adsorption of IpaD onto silica gels. Then the silica-IpaD complex is heated above the denaturing temperature of the protein to determine if the silica gel maintains the secondary structure of IpaD during heating. These proteins are then removed using N,N-Dimethyldodecylamine N-oxide (LDAO) detergent, and their secondary structure is tested using circular dichroism. The results demonstrate that silica gel maintains a high percentage of the native unheated alpha-helical structure of IpaD, thereby maintaining vaccine potency.

title: pH-Dependent Degradation of Poly(ethylene oxide)- Block -Polycaprolactone Films
abstract: Currently 90% of pharmaceuticals in the discovery pipeline are hydrophobic, yet such hydrophobic compounds account for only 40% of drugs that are FDA-approved and marketable. Consequently, researchers recognize that there is an urgent need for better delivery mechanisms for hydrophobic drugs to increase efficacy and reduce negative side-effects. Poly(ethylene oxide)-block-polycaprolactone (PEO- b -PCL) is an FDA-approved, biocompatible, amphiphilic block copolymer, making it an intriguing candidate for hydrophobic drug encapsulation and controlled release into the body. In this work, a variety of characterization techniques, including DSC, NMR, and SEM, are employed to investigate the degradation of PEO- b -PCL films within aquatic environments. Previous work shows that the degradation of these films is accelerated in both basic and acidic environments, however there are opportunities to better understand the degradation rate as it relates to the physical structure of the films. This information suggests that pH could be used as an external stimulus to guide the release of hydrophobic compounds encapsulated within the PCL. Through examining the effect of block fraction and crystallinity on the degradation rate and pathway at various pH, the potential of PEO- b -PCL as a delivery agent can be better understood.

title: Powering Clean Energy with Seawater: Understanding the Selectivity of Oxygen/Chlorine Evolution for Metal Catalysts
abstract: Energy is a globally valued resource. In order to meet energy demands in the face of climate change, finding new methods to store renewable energies is essential. A clean method to store energy is through the electrolysis of water. Such a reaction can be driven by renewable energy sources like solar energy. In this project, an abundant resource is explored as an electrolyte to store energy — seawater. Seawater contains many different salts, often salts containing chlorides. The electrolysis of water evolves hydrogen and oxygen gas, which can act as fuels when recombined in a fuel cell to generate electricity, heat, and desalinated water; however, the addition of chloride containing salts in the electrolyte results in the evolution of chlorine gas, a toxic byproduct, competing with oxygen evolution reaction. The goal in electrolysis of artificial seawater is to understand and control an electrode’s selectivity towards oxygen evolution by analyzing an electrode’s performance via cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry. By comparing the performance of various electrodes, earth-abundant metals with high catalytic activity towards oxygen evolution over chlorine evolution can be confirmed, and a greater understanding of what materials are efficient and selective towards oxygen evolution can be reached. With this understanding comes better electrode designs in the future to improve selectivity towards oxygen evolution. In this project, the tested electrodes have been developed by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, the Epitaxial Complex Oxide Lab from Sungkyunkwan University, and in Dr. Kelsey Stoerzinger’s lab from drop casting and electrodeposition.

title: Computational Studies of the Self-Assembly of Tapered Brush-Coil Polymers in Solution
abstract: Materials formed by the assembly of block copolymers have many applications in environmental cleanup, drug delivery, electronics, optics, etc. In the past, block copolymers with linear architecture have been studied extensively using experiments and simulations. Moving to non-linear architectures, such as star, bottlebrush, and brush-coil, has the potential to advance assembly studies by producing new trends in structure and thermodynamics not seen in linear systems. One specific architecture of interest to us is a tapered brush-coil where the solvophobic polymer block has a bottlebrush architecture of varying density and gradient of side chain length, and the solvophilic polymer block has a linear architecture. In this poster, I will present my recent work, focused on the assembly in tapered brush-coil polymer solutions using a coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation. For varying grafting density of side chain, gradient, and the direction of gradient of side chain length, I compare the assembled micelle size, aggregation number, and concentration profiles. At low grafting densities, there are observable differences in micelle size between a positive and negative gradient. At high grafting densities the micelle sizes are statistically similar for both gradient directions; however, the chains pack differently within the micelles. This packing is done in a way that does not drastically alter the concentration profile of the micellar core between grafting densities. This implies that while the bulk properties of the micelles may be similar, their internal composition and properties are completely different.

title: Phase Transitions of Titanium Dioxide Nanocrystals
abstract: Titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) is a widely-used catalyst with three distinct nanocrystal phases – anatase, rutile, and brookite. The chemical properties and catalytic activity of TiO 2 vary with its crystal phase, making morphology an important determining factor in catalytic performance. A synthesis method involving thermal hydrolysis of a titanium precursor solution in the presence of urea was implemented for the direct synthesis of anatase and brookite, while rutile was produced through the high-temperature calcination of anatase and brookite materials. The anatase-to-rutile transition (ART) was investigated as a function of both calcination temperature and time to gain an understanding of how those factors affect TiO 2 phase transition. Our results revealed that partial transitions occurred in the 450-550°C range. This temperature range also makes it possible to produce customized mixtures of the anatase, brookite, and rutile phases.

title: Creation of 3D Ordered Superlattices through Self-Assembly of Polymer-Functionalized Nanoparticles
abstract: Functional nanomaterial assemblies are an exciting area of study with various applications across catalysis, photonics, electronics, plasmonics, and biomedical applications. We focused on the study of metamaterials that can show electromagnetic properties not observed in nature with specific interest in their unique optical properties. Using gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) as a model for other metallic nanoshapes, we demonstrated that the respective functionalization of these nanoparticles with poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether thiol (PEG-SH) and poly(acrylic acid)-thiol (PAA-SH) to form AuNP-PEG and AuNP-PAA core-shell nanoparticles allows for a bridge to be created between neighboring nanoparticles. These bridges were formed through the addition of free polymers in solutions of AuNP-PEG nanoparticles and inter-chain hydrogen bonding between protonated poly(acrylic acid) chains in the shells of AuNP-PAA nanoparticles. We demonstrate that these functionalized nanoparticles self-assemble into 3D ordered structures in bulk solution similar to programmable assembly using complementary DNA strands through the use of synchrotron small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and various optical characterization techniques. The effect of pH, salt concentration, PEG and PAA chains on the inter-particle distances in the assemblies will be discussed. Facile implementation of block copolymer based self-assembly techniques is enabled by substituting simpler synthetic polymers instead of DNA and the results showed that these superlattices are stabilized by vanderWaals forces, and that allows the structures to be stable even when removed from the aqueous solutions.

title: Melting Temperature Effects on the Crystallization Order of PEO-b-PCL Copolymers
abstract: Various samples of poly(ethylene oxide)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone) (PEO-b-PCL) of different molecular weights were dissolved either in toluene or chloroform, melted at different temperatures, and cooled to investigate which block would crystallize first. Depending on which block crystallizes first, it may crystallize more thereby influencing the macroscopic properties of the copolymer film. Analysis was conducted using Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and FTIR. Previous observations have indicated that during evaporation crystallization, the polymer film preferentially crystallizes PCL first but under certain conditions, PEO crystallizes first. These conditions included but were not limited to the solvent used to solvate the film and the molecular weight of each block. So, the goal of this project was to investigate whether the melting temperature influences the order of crystallization of the film. In doing so, the researcher is ultimately trying to find out if it is possible to control the properties of the polymer film.

title: Waste Biomass-Derived Anode for Application in Superior Lithium Ion Batteries
abstract: Given the simultaneous demand for lithium-ion batteries and environmentally-friendly practices, there is a distinct opportunity for batteries derived from waste biomass. Carbonaceous battery anodes synthesized from avocado seeds upcycles a completely valueless waste material into a highly demanded product. The novel electrode demonstrates promising performance, outperforming graphite at every applied current density from 25 mAg -1 to 400 mAg -1 . The novel electrode performs comparably to graphene electrodes in terms of cycling (315 mAhg -1 at 100 mAg -1 ) but does not share graphene’s instability at high (400 mAg -1 ) applied current densities. By characterizing the material using X-ray Powder Diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, BET analysis, and extensive cyclic voltammetry, the amorphousness of the biomass-derived anode was found to contribute 54% of lithium storage to capacitance-driven mechanisms, compared to 35% in graphite and graphene. However, the high amorphousness and high surface area facilitates the formation of a large solid-electrolyte interphase, causing a significant first-cycle irreversible capacity loss. Despite this, its combined superior performance and environmentally-friendly nature causes the presented anode to be a practical upgrade from the current commercial graphite anode.

title: Processing of Nanostructured Block Copolymer Micelle Crystals
abstract: Block copolymers in solvents that are selective to one block form intricate nanostructures that can give rise to useful material properties. The mechanical properties of the crystalline phases seen in concentrated block copolymer solutions depend on nanoscale structure and sample history. In this work, the phase behavior of a triblock polymer, Pluronic P123 (PEO 20 -PPO 70 -PEO 20 ), and water system was studied. These liquid crystals undergo a thermoreversible transition from a liquid-like disordered state at low temperatures (T < 15 °C) into a gel-like soft solid at higher temperatures (T > 20 °C). The goal of this work is to characterize the thermotropic and concentration-dependent mechanical behavior of this system in order to elucidate the nanoscale structures in the P123 and water system and inform future structural studies. We are interested in determining the impact of processing on the nanoscale structure and resulting mechanical properties of these materials. To construct a phase diagram for the P123 and water system, inversion tests were first conducted to distinguish the disordered and ordered states. Samples with visible changes in appearance and viscosity with temperature were identified as target concentrations for rheological study. Subsequent rheometric temperature sweeps were conducted on these target concentrations to locate changes in modulus that may signify structural changes with temperature. Currently, we are working to develop a method to quantify birefringence under shear to distinguish isotropic phases, which exhibit no birefringence, from anisotropic lamellar and hexagonal phases, which are birefringent to different extents. A motivation for this research is the potential application of P123 in drug-delivery systems. Due to its non-toxicity and low-temperature disordering, this polymer could potentially encase therapeutic enzymes throughout the water-filled interstitial spaces. This could facilitate storage of these therapeutic proteins without refrigeration. It is important to understand the impact of processing on these materials so that the desired structures and material properties can be achieved.

title: Formulation of a Fiber Reinforced Silicon Carbide Colloidal Gel Ink for Direct Ink Writing and Unassisted Sintering
abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) is an advanced ceramic material made desirable by its low cost, high hardness, and excellent durability. For these reasons, it is used in a wide variety of applications including ceramic plates in ballistic vests, brake surfaces for cars, and abrasive tools for grinding. However, SiC is susceptible to cracking and ultimately failure due to a lack of plastic deformation, leading to low toughness. Here, a SiC fiber reinforced composite (FRC) material was made into a colloidal gel ink for direct ink writing (DIW) and sintering. DIW enables the fabrication of parts with complex geometries that are difficult or impossible to make with conventional pressing methods, as well as the ability to do rapid prototyping. In this work, 30 vol% SiC whiskers are added to SiC particles to toughen the resulting SiC matrix, while yttrium oxide (Y 2 O 3 ) and aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 ) were added in small quantities as sintering aids. The solid ceramic particles were suspended in water using a polyelectrolyte dispersant, and an oppositely charged polyelectrolyte was used as a flocculant. A viscosifier was used to increase ink viscosity and prevent ink phase separation. An ink formulation (>45% by volume solids) has been developed that exhibits shear thinning behavior and has high solids loading. Push-rod dilatometry was used to characterize the densification behavior of the printed part during unassisted sintering. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to characterize the microstructure after sintering, and to determine if whisker fracture occurred during ink processing or printing.

title: Residence Time Distribution and Specific Mechanical Energy in Solid-State Shear Pulverization: Processing-Structure Relationships in a Chilled Twin-Screw Extruder
abstract: Solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP) is a continuous polymer processing methodology based on a modified twin screw extruder. The unique application of low barrel temperatures and mechanochemistry have contributed to the development of an extensive range of polymer-based materials, from environmentally responsible polymer blends to nanocomposites, for more than 30 years. The complex processing-structure-processing relationships in SSSP can be elucidated by evaluating the interplay between numerous processing parameters using integrated, measured covariants. Residence time distribution and specific mechanical energy are evaluated in a base case polypropylene study under a full factorial experiment involving screw design, screw speed, and throughput parameters. These factors are in turn correlated to dispersion morphology and thermal property results from a parallel study based on a model polypropylene/carbon black composite. This investigation highlights the tunability of SSSP processing parameters for tailored output with desired purposes and applications. In particular, enhanced residence distribution can be achieved with low screw speed and high throughput settings, leading to high levels of material mixing and shear.

title: The Study of Segregation of Dyes in PEO- B -PCL
abstract: As an amphiphilic biodegradable copolymer, PEO- b -PCL is useful for many biomedical applications. The segregation of medicine in the PEO- b -PCL has implication on the release rate of medicine inside a biological system. The objective of the project is to study the segregation of medicine in PEO(5000)- b -PCL(16300) diblock copolymer using azobenzene dyes and bromophenol blue to mimic the presence of the medication. PEO(5000)- b -PCL(16300) films were integrated with methyl yellow, methyl red and bromophenol blue dyes with different mass ratio to determine the effect of dyes concentration on the physical and chemical properties of the copolymer including melting point, crystallization temperature and percent crystallinity of each block. As shown by DSC analysis, the melting point and the crystallization point of PEO- b -PCL both decreased as the concentration of bromophenol blue increased while they both increased as the concentration of methyl red increased. Also, both DSC and ATR-FTIR data showed that the percent crystallinity of PEO block was influenced by the presence of methyl red. However, methyl yellow had no significant influence on the melting point and crystallization point of the PEO- b -PCL. The preliminary results for the dyes segregation in PEO- b -PCL films are: methyl red mostly in PEO block; bromophenol blue distributed among PEO and PCL blocks and methyl yellow stay on the surface of the films.

title: Degradation Induced Shape Recovery of Anhydride-Based Shape Memory Polymer Composite
abstract: Shape memory polymers (SMP) are smart polymeric materials that can recover from a temporary shape to their permanent shape in response to an external stimulus. The permanent shape is achieved through physical or chemical crosslinks, while the temporary shape is a result of deformation and immobilization of the polymer chains. SMPs have become high in demand due to their many applications, ranging from medical devices and actuators to smart adhesives and sensors. We have recently created a reconfigurable shape memory elastomeric composite (Re-SMEC) featuring a water-degradable, elastomeric polyanhydride (PAH) matrix as the fixing phase, and elastic fibers as the permanent, memory retaining phase. This project explores the recovery of the original shape as a response to the degradation of the matrix. The morphology, mechanical properties, phase transitions, and degradation profile are reported.

title: Gelation of Hyaluronic Acid for Drug Delivery and Tissue Engineering Applications
abstract: Hyaluronic acid (HA) is a naturally occurring biopolymer found in most vertebrates that regulates cell migration, differentiation, inflammation responses, and angiogenesis. Crosslinking of HA improves mechanical properties and can increase the stability in water, making HA an ideal candidate for drug delivery and tissue engineering applications. Here, methacrylated hyaluronic acid (MeHA) was synthesized to add functional groups for crosslinking purposes and dithiothreitol (DTT) was used to crosslink the HA into a hydrogel. Control of crosslinking of HA in solution yields nanogels suitable for drug delivery, or macroscopic gels useful as tissue scaffolds. A fluorescent tag was added to enable quantification of HA nanogel concentration. Fluorescence spectrometry of samples with varying ratios of fluorescent methacrylated hyaluronic acid (Fl-MeHA) to MeHA revealed a linear correlation between fluorescence intensity and the concentration of Fl-MeHA. In addition, oscillatory rheology was used to determine the stiffness of 3 wt% MeHA gels using various concentrations of DTT crosslinker, and these experiments revealed that gels exhibited varying stiffness over time. These preliminary results show that hyaluronic acid gels have the potential to be used in a variety of contexts including drug delivery and in vitro model systems.

title: Recyclable Shape-Memory Elastomers
abstract: Shape-memory (SM) polymers are an important class of materials with a wide range of application areas, including biotechnology, textiles, and aerospace engineering. These materials undergo triggered actuation from kinetically metastable deformed states to their original, or permanent, shapes. Semicrystalline SM materials with complete shape-recovery conventionally require covalent crosslinks, thereby precluding melt-processing and recycling. Typical SM polymers are thus constrained to one shape-specific application per product and inherently limited in the sustainability of their life cycles. The objective of this project is to replace covalent crosslinks with strong and reversible hydrogen bonding interactions to enable melt-processable SM polymers without sacrificing performance. Two high molecular weight melt-processable systems have been successfully synthesized, with excellent SM fixities and strain recovery before and after processing. Dynamic mechanical analysis reveals a stiffness plateau that extends over a large temperature range (60-170°C) that is well above the shape-triggering temperature (~50°C). Stress relaxation studies suggest that chain (dis)entanglement kinetics strongly influence the materials’ viscoelastic behavior, including the conditions of temperature and stress under which viscous flow is achieved. Dynamic, time-resolved, isothermal experiments building on these results will better illuminate the relationship between environmental conditioning and stress decay timescales and how it can be used to optimize processing conditions. The role of interchain H-bond strength in determining thermomechanical behavior at high temperatures is also currently being investigated through the use of linkage groups with weaker regimes of interchain association strength.

title: Permeability of Cured Composite Skins Produced Using Co-Cure over Honeycomb Core
abstract: Honeycomb sandwich structures made of fiber-reinforced polymer facesheets, film adhesive, and core can be produced using co-cure, during which the facesheets and adhesive are processed simultaneously. Frequently, honeycomb skins (facesheets and adhesive) must be impermeable during service to protect the core from environmental degradation or maintain internal pressure. However, skins can be rendered permeable by process-induced defects such as porosity. This paper describes an investigation of relationships between process conditions during co-cure and skin permeability. Half-sandwich structures composed of a four-ply prepreg laminate, a layer of film adhesive, and a honeycomb core were fabricated using a custom designed lab-scale fixture and controlled thermal and pressure conditions. Autoclave, bag, and core pressures were varied to evaluate hypotheses about mechanisms leading to permeability. Parts were cured with vacuum drawn in the bag and core (resulting in porosity), with super-ambient bag and core pressures (leading to minimal porosity), or with several constant pressure gradients between bag and core (leading to possible continuous flow between these regions). The resulting skins were tested for permeability within a second custom-designed fixture that allowed accurate, repeatable gas flow rate measurements across the skins. Gas flow pathways were also located using a water layer. The micro-structure of the skins was analyzed using light microscopy of polished sections to assess the presence, amount, location, and distribution of porosity and other defects. Results showed that porosity is related to permeability, but that gas flow through skins is possible even without high void contents. Pressure differentials led to complex variations in permeability, showing that variations in gas flow rate between cured skins is at least partly stochastic. Overall, the study contributes to a fundamental understanding of processing and manufacturing science for composites, and can provide useful guidelines for improving manufacturing processes and ensuring part quality.

title: Poly(l-lactic acid) Nanoparticles Produced By Impingement Jet Mixing Solvent Displacement: Optimization of Process Parameters for Particle Size and Polydispersity
abstract: Many researchers are concentrating on developing polymer nanoparticles for controlled drug delivery because they are small enough to diffuse through tissues, target to specific tissues and in some cases, penetrate through cell membranes to deliver the drug more locally, mitigating side effects seen with intravenous injection. There are still difficulties in producing polymer nanoparticles at scale and in a size range (60 to 80 nm in diameter) that are large enough to avoid many of the biological barriers such as macrophages and other immune cells, and yet small enough to have reasonable diffusion rates through tissue. Another outstanding issue is to find out how the polymer nanoparticles can be purified from excess surfactant used when making the particles. In this work, we looked at the effect of process parameters (amount of surfactant, location of surfactant, quench volume, and flow rate) on the polymer nanoparticle diameter produced with impingement jets mixing in a batch-fed process through solvent displacement. Solvent displacement uses a solvent for the polymer that is miscible with water. When the polymer solution mixes with water, the polymer precipitates and the solvent diffuses into the water. Excess surfactant is added to stabilize the polymer nanoparticles in order to prevent aggregation. We find that the quench volume and the surfactant concentration have the biggest effect on polymer nanoparticle diameter and the other parameters have little effect.
